**SECTION THREE: PHILOSOPHICAL PROBLEMS**

Is death the end of human existence?

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** Death is the end of biological life, but philosophers ask whether it is also the end of the person, that is, whether something of the human being survives. The problematic is whether human existence stops entirely at death, or whether the soul, the person or the spirit continues in some form.

**Thesis: death is the end of human existence.**
(i) *Materialism.* Epicurus and the atomists held that the soul, like the body, is made of atoms which disperse at death. Epicurus added that death is nothing to us: when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not. Modern materialism and neuroscience tie consciousness to brain activity: when the brain stops, consciousness stops.
(ii) *Empiricism.* Hume noted that we have no experience of a soul apart from the body and no evidence of survival, so the belief is not supported by reason.
(iii) *Dependence of mind on body.* Memory, character and thought change with injury, drugs or illness, which suggests that the mind depends on the body.
(iv) *Existentialist reading.* For Sartre death is not a gate to another life but the end of the possibilities of the person, absurd and outside any project; for Heidegger, man is a being-toward-death, whose finitude gives life its seriousness and urgency, without a promise of survival.

**Antithesis: death is not the end.**
(i) *The immortality of the soul.* Plato (in the *Phaedo*) argued that the soul is simple, akin to the eternal Forms, and therefore outlasts the body, which is composite. Descartes held that the mind is a distinct, thinking substance, separable from the body. Kant presented the immortality of the soul as a postulate of practical reason, needed so that virtue may be proportioned to happiness.
(ii) *Religious doctrines.* Christianity and Islam teach resurrection and judgment; Hinduism and Buddhism teach rebirth. These doctrines rest on faith and revelation.
(iii) *African thought.* Many African traditions hold that death is a passage: the dead become ancestors, called by Mbiti the living-dead, who remain members of the community as long as they are remembered, and may be reborn in the family. Life is a continuous circle that includes the ancestors.
(iv) *Objections to materialism.* Critics say it does not explain consciousness, personal identity and freedom, and that the argument from dependence on the brain only shows that the mind is conditioned by the body, not that it is identical to it.

**Synthesis.** The question mixes what can be shown by experience (death ends bodily life and the functions of the brain) with what depends on metaphysical or religious belief (whether something survives). Neither position can be demonstrated conclusively. What the options share is that the thought of death makes us consider the value of life and of how it is lived.

**Conclusion.** Philosophy cannot prove with certainty that death is, or is not, the end of human existence. The materialist and existentialist answer is the best supported by observation; the dualist, religious and African answers are supported by arguments about the soul and by faith. A reasonable position acknowledges the limits of proof and treats the question as one on which the arguments are balanced.

**SECTION THREE: PHILOSOPHICAL PROBLEMS**

Can man be held responsible for his acts?

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** To hold someone responsible is to judge that he is the author of his act and so deserves praise or blame, reward or punishment. This presupposes that he could have acted otherwise, that is, that he is free. The problematic is whether man, who is subject to nature, heredity, upbringing and society, can really be held responsible for his acts.

**Thesis: man can be held responsible.**
(i) *Freedom of the will.* Libertarians, such as Sartre, hold that man is free: existence precedes essence, man makes himself by his choices and cannot hide behind excuses, for even refusing to choose is a choice. Kant holds that, as a rational being, man is able to follow the moral law, and the very sense of duty (you ought, therefore you can) shows that he is free.
(ii) *Voluntary acts.* Aristotle distinguishes voluntary acts, which have their origin in the agent who knows what he does, from involuntary ones, done through force or ignorance. For voluntary acts, including those of character built by habit, man is responsible.
(iii) *Social necessity.* Without responsibility there would be no morality, law, justice or punishment, and no praise for good conduct. Society treats persons as accountable; it is a condition of living together.
(iv) *Conscience.* We feel guilt, remorse and pride about our acts, which shows that we regard ourselves as their authors.

**Antithesis: man cannot (fully) be held responsible.**
(i) *Determinism.* Spinoza and, in different forms, modern science hold that every event has causes. If our choices are caused by heredity, environment, unconscious drives (Freud) and social conditions (Marx), then the feeling of freedom is an illusion, as Spinoza said of a stone that thinks it flies freely.
(ii) *Limits of responsibility.* Even the law recognises that children, the insane, and persons acting under constraint, threat or ignorance are not or are less responsible. Passion, addiction, poverty and manipulation reduce freedom.
(iii) *Fate.* Some religious doctrines of predestination, and some Greek and African ideas of destiny, suggest that the outcome of our acts is not wholly in our control.
(iv) *Punishment.* If acts are determined, blame is unjust and punishment should aim at reform or protection, not retribution.

**Synthesis.** Compatibilists such as Hume and Mill reconcile the two: freedom is not absence of causes but acting from one's own motives without external compulsion, so a person can be responsible for acts that flow from his character and choices, even if these have causes. Responsibility is then a matter of degree: it is full when the act is voluntary, informed and uncoerced, and reduced by constraint, ignorance or illness.

**Conclusion.** Man can be held responsible for his acts, but within limits. Total responsibility ignores the weight of conditioning, and total determinism removes the basis of morality and law. The most defensible view is that man is responsible to the extent that he acts knowingly and freely, and that society should judge each case by this measure.

b) more positive charge carriers

b) Beta particles

**Exercice 1 (5 points)**

**a.** State

(i) Faraday's law of electromagnetism. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Lenz's law of electromagnetism. *[1 mark]*

**b.** A transformer in a radio set delivers $5\,\mathrm{A}$ at a voltage of $6\,\mathrm{V}$ from a socket connected to a $240\,\mathrm{V}$ line.

(i) State whether this transformer is a step up or a step down transformer. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the amount of current that enters the socket. *[2 marks]*

**a.** State

(i) Faraday's law of electromagnetism. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Lenz's law of electromagnetism. *[1 mark]*

(i) **Faraday's law:** the magnitude of the e.m.f. induced in a conductor (or coil) is **directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage**, that is, to the rate at which the conductor cuts magnetic field lines.

(ii) **Lenz's law:** the **direction of the induced current (or e.m.f.) is always such that it opposes the change that produces it**.

[COURS_LINK:electromagnetic-induction-from-moving-magnets-to-transformers]

**b.** A transformer in a radio set delivers $5\,\mathrm{A}$ at a voltage of $6\,\mathrm{V}$ from a socket connected to a $240\,\mathrm{V}$ line.

(i) State whether this transformer is a step up or a step down transformer. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the amount of current that enters the socket. *[2 marks]*

(i) The transformer receives $240\,\mathrm{V}$ and delivers only $6\,\mathrm{V}$. The output voltage is smaller than the input voltage, so it is a **step down transformer**.

(ii) For a $100\%$ efficient transformer, power in = power out:

$V_pI_p=V_sI_s$

$I_p=\dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{6\,\mathrm{V}\times5\,\mathrm{A}}{240\,\mathrm{V}}=\dfrac{30\,\mathrm{W}}{240\,\mathrm{V}}=0.125\,\mathrm{A}$

**The current entering the socket (primary current) is $0.125\,\mathrm{A}$.**

**Exercice 2 (6 points)**

**a.** State the law of conservation of linear momentum. *[2 marks]*

**b.** A car of mass $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ is travelling at $60\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(i) Calculate its momentum. *[2 marks]*

(ii) If it crashes into a wall and is brought to rest in $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$, calculate the force it exerts on the wall. *[2 marks]*

**a.** State the law of conservation of linear momentum. *[2 marks]*

The **law of conservation of linear momentum** states that, **for a closed (isolated) system on which no external force acts, the total linear momentum before a collision (or interaction) is equal to the total linear momentum after it**.

[COURS_LINK:linear-momentum-conservation-recoil-and-impulse]

**b.** A car of mass $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ is travelling at $60\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(i) Calculate its momentum. *[2 marks]*

(ii) If it crashes into a wall and is brought to rest in $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$, calculate the force it exerts on the wall. *[2 marks]*

(i) $\text{momentum}=mv=1000\,\mathrm{kg}\times60\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}=6.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

(ii) The force equals the rate of change of momentum:

$F=\dfrac{mv-mu}{t}=\dfrac{0-60\,000}{0.5}=-1.2\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N}$

The minus sign only shows that the wall stops the car. By Newton's third law the car exerts on the wall a force of the same size: **$1.2\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{N}$ ($120\,000\,\mathrm{N}$)**.

(i) Any two of: the **length** of the conductor (resistance increases with length); its **cross-sectional area** (resistance decreases when the wire is thicker); the **material** it is made of (its resistivity); its **temperature**.

(ii) The $3\,\Omega$ and $2\,\Omega$ resistors are in parallel:

$R_{\parallel}=\dfrac{3\times2}{3+2}=1.2\,\Omega$

This combination is in series with the $5\,\Omega$ resistor:

$R_{\text{total}}=5+1.2=6.2\,\Omega$

**The total resistance is $6.2\,\Omega$.**

(iii) The $5\,\Omega$ resistor is in series with the rest of the circuit, so it carries the whole current from the $6\,\mathrm{V}$ cell:

$I=\dfrac{V}{R_{\text{total}}}=\dfrac{6}{6.2}=0.97\,\mathrm{A}$

**Apparatus:** a rectangular glass block, a soft-board (drawing board), a white sheet of paper, drawing pins, four optical (search) pins, a sharp pencil, a protractor, a ruler, a set square.

**Diagram of the set-up** (described): the paper is pinned on the soft-board and the glass block lies on it. Its outline $ABCD$ is drawn. A normal $NN'$ is drawn at point $O$ on face $AB$. A line $PO$ making an angle $i$ with the normal represents the incident ray. Pins $P_1$ and $P_2$ are stuck upright on the line $PO$, about $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart. Looking through face $CD$, pins $P_3$ and $P_4$ are placed so that the four pins appear exactly in line. The line through $P_3$ and $P_4$ meets $CD$ at $O'$. Join $O$ to $O'$: this is the ray inside the glass.

**Procedure:** (1) Fix the paper, place the block and trace its outline. (2) Draw the normal at $O$ and the incident line making an angle $i$ (for example $30^\circ$) with it. (3) Fix $P_1$ and $P_2$ on the incident line. (4) Looking through the opposite face, fix $P_3$ and $P_4$ so that they hide the images of $P_1$ and $P_2$ (all four in line). (5) Remove the block and the pins, draw the emergent line through $P_3$, $P_4$ and join $O$ to $O'$. (6) Draw the normal at $O$ on the inside of the glass and measure the angle of refraction $r$ (the angle between $OO'$ and the normal). (7) Calculate $n=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$. (8) Repeat for other angles of incidence ($20^\circ, 40^\circ, 50^\circ, 60^\circ$), then take the mean of $n$ or plot $\sin i$ against $\sin r$: the gradient is $n$.

**Precautions:** the pins must be fixed **vertically** and **far apart** (at least $5\,\mathrm{cm}$) to give an accurate line; use a **sharp pencil** and a thin outline; keep the block **still** while tracing and sighting; look at the **bases of the pins** when aligning them; do not use too small or too large angles of incidence; keep the eye at table level; use a **protractor with care**, reading to the nearest degree.

- **Isotopes:** atoms of the **same element** (same proton number $Z$) that have **different numbers of neutrons**, so different mass numbers.
- **Half-life:** the **time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay** (equivalently, for the activity or count rate to fall to half).
- **Transmutation:** the **change of one element into another** when a nucleus emits a particle. In alpha decay the proton number falls by $2$ and the mass number by $4$: $^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}\rightarrow{}^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po}+{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$.

**e.** Alpha particle tracks in a cloud chamber are **thick**, **straight** and **short**, while beta-particles tracks are **thin**, **wavy** and **long**. State the reason for each of the characteristics underlined above. *[6 marks]*

**Alpha tracks**

- **Thick:** an alpha particle has a **large charge ($+2$) and a large mass**, so it is **strongly ionising**: it produces many ions per millimetre of path, and the droplets that form on them make a thick track.
- **Straight:** an alpha particle is **heavy**, so collisions with air molecules hardly deflect it.
- **Short:** because it ionises so strongly it **loses its energy quickly**, so it travels only a few centimetres in air.

**Beta tracks**

- **Thin:** a beta particle has a **small charge ($-1$) and a very small mass** and moves very fast, so it is **weakly ionising** and produces few ions per millimetre.
- **Wavy:** it is **very light**, so collisions with air molecules **deflect it easily** and it changes direction.
- **Long:** because it ionises weakly it **loses energy slowly** and travels much farther (metres in air) before it stops.

(i) The ball moves **towards the rod** (to the right in Figure 4): it is attracted.

(ii) A force of **electrostatic attraction**.

(iii) The **size of the charges** (the larger the charge on the rod or the ball, the larger the force) and the **distance between them** (the force decreases when the distance increases). The medium between them also matters.

(iv) The negative rod **repels the free electrons** of the metal coating of the ball, which move to the **side of the ball farthest from the rod**. The **near side is left with a positive charge** (induced charge) and the far side is negative. The attraction between the rod and the nearer, positive side is **stronger than the repulsion** from the farther, negative side (the force is larger at a smaller distance). The net force on the ball is therefore an attraction, and the ball moves towards the rod.

(v) **Polythene is an insulator**: the charge produced by rubbing stays where it is made and cannot flow away. **Copper is a conductor**: the charge produced by rubbing flows through the rod and the hand to the earth, so a copper rod held in the hand cannot be charged (unless it is held with an insulating handle).

**d.** List two ways by which electrical energy could be lost in a transformer and in each case explain how this loss could be minimised. *[4 marks]*

1. **Heating of the coils (resistance of the windings, $I^2R$ loss):** the current heats the copper wire. It is minimised by **using thick copper wire of low resistance** for the coils (especially the low-voltage, high-current coil).

2. **Eddy currents in the iron core:** the changing magnetic flux induces currents in the core, which heat it. They are minimised by **making the core of thin, insulated sheets (laminations)** instead of a solid block.

(Other accepted losses: **hysteresis** loss, minimised by using a **soft iron core** that is easily magnetised and demagnetised; **flux leakage**, minimised by winding the secondary coil **on top of the primary** on a closed core.)

**e.** Figure 6.0 shows a conductor AB placed in the magnetic field, N-S of two magnets and connected to a centre-zero galvanometer.

(i) Explain why the galvanometer deflects? *[3 marks]*

(ii) If the direction of movement of the conductor is reversed, state and explain what is observed on the galvanometer. *[3 marks]*

(iii) State two factors that determine the magnitude of deflection. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Name any rule that could be used to determine the direction of the magnetic field lines about the straight current A carrying conductor. *[1 mark]*

(i) When the conductor AB is moved upwards between the poles, it **cuts the magnetic field lines** (the magnetic flux linked with the circuit changes). By **electromagnetic induction** an **e.m.f. is induced** in AB. Because AB is part of a **closed circuit** with the galvanometer, an **induced current flows** and the pointer deflects.

(ii) The pointer **deflects in the opposite direction** (to the other side of the zero). When the direction of motion of the conductor is reversed, the **direction of the induced e.m.f. and current is reversed** (Fleming's right-hand rule / Lenz's law: the induced current always opposes the motion, so changing the motion changes its direction).

(iii) Any two of: the **speed** at which the conductor is moved; the **strength of the magnetic field (strength of the magnets)**; the **length of the conductor** in the field (or the number of turns if it is a coil).

(iv) The **right-hand grip rule** (Maxwell's corkscrew rule): grip the conductor with the right hand, thumb pointing along the current; the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines.

Figure 7.0 shows three rectangular metal blocks A, B, and C. Block A is a permanent magnet of known polarity, B is a magnetic material and C another permanent magnet.

![Three rectangular blocks A (marked N at the left end and S at the right end), B and C (unmarked).](/media/figures/cm/gce-ol-physics-2018-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_4.webp)

*Figure 7*

Explain how you would use block A to show a group of form 5 students that B is a magnetic material and C a permanent magnet. *[3 marks]*

**Hard and soft magnetic materials**

- A **hard magnetic material** is **difficult to magnetise but keeps its magnetism for a long time** (it is hard to demagnetise). Example: **steel** (also alnico, cobalt steel). It is used for permanent magnets.
- A **soft magnetic material** is **easily magnetised and easily demagnetised**: it loses its magnetism as soon as the magnetising field is removed. Example: **soft iron**. It is used for the cores of electromagnets and transformers.

**Using block A (a bar magnet, N at the left end and S at the right end)**

- **To show that C is a permanent magnet:** bring the **north pole of A near one end of C, then near the other end**. A permanent magnet will **repel** at one of its ends (like poles repel) and attract at the other. Repulsion is the only sure test for a magnet.
- **To show that B is a magnetic material (not a magnet):** bring the same pole of A near **each end of B in turn**. B is **attracted at both ends** and is **never repelled**; B is a magnetic material that becomes an induced magnet (nearest end gets an opposite pole) and loses its magnetism when A is removed.

c) $x-3y=0$
d) $x+3y=0$

A line through the origin is invariant if its direction vector is an eigenvector of $M$. c) A reflection in the $x$-axis
d) A reflection in the $y$-axis

Apply $M$ to a point: $M\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\-y\end{pmatrix}$. The $x$-coordinate is unchanged and the $y$-coordinate changes sign, which is a reflection in the $x$-axis. A rotation through $90^\circ$ would have matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&\mp1\\\pm1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and a reflection in the $y$-axis would be $\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. **Answer: C.**

**1.** Which of the following is the main function of collenchyma and sclerenchyma in plants?

a) Storage.
b) Support.
c) Transport of water.
d) Transport of food.

Collenchyma (living, with cellulose thickening at the corners) supports young stems and petioles, and sclerenchyma (dead, with lignified walls) gives rigidity and strength to mature organs. Neither stores food, and the transport of water and of food is done by xylem and phloem. Their main function is support. **Answer: B.**

**2.** The inhibition of lateral buds by the presence of shoot tips is called:

a) grafting.
b) cuttings.
c) apical dominance.
d) marcotting.

The shoot apex produces auxin (IAA), which moves down the stem and inhibits the growth of the axillary (lateral) buds, so the plant grows tall and unbranched. This is apical dominance. When the tip is removed the lateral buds grow. Grafting, cuttings and marcotting (air layering) are methods of artificial vegetative propagation. **Answer: C.**

**3.** Impulses to the Purkinje tissue take rise from the:

a) atrio-ventricular node (AVN).
b) sino-atrial node (SAN).
c) brain.
d) vagus nerve.

The sino-atrial node (SAN) starts each heartbeat and the wave of excitation spreads over the atria to the atrio-ventricular node (AVN). After a short delay the AVN passes the impulse down the bundle of His and its branches to the Purkinje fibres in the ventricular walls, which make the ventricles contract from the apex upwards. The impulse to the Purkinje tissue therefore comes from the AVN (via the bundle of His). The SAN acts only at the start of the chain, and the brain and the vagus nerve only modify the rate. **Answer: A.**

**4.** Which of the following takes place during inspiration?

a) The external intercostal muscles contract and ribs are moved upwards and outwards.
b) The internal intercostal muscles relax and ribs move inwards and downwards.
c) The external intercostal muscles relax and ribs move downwards and inwards.
d) The internal intercostal muscles contract and ribs move upwards and outwards.

During inspiration the external intercostal muscles contract while the internal intercostals relax, so the ribs move upwards and outwards, and the diaphragm contracts and flattens. The volume of the thorax increases, the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. Options B, C and D describe the relaxation of the external intercostals or the contraction of the internal ones, which belongs to expiration. **Answer: A.**

**5.** Which of the following is associated with nitrogen fixation in bacterial cells?

a) Bacterial chromosomes.
b) Photosynthetic membranes.
c) Plasmids.
d) Pilli.

The genes for nitrogen fixation (the nif genes) of nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium are carried on plasmids (the symbiotic plasmid), and plasmids are the vectors used to transfer these genes between bacteria. The photosynthetic membranes belong to photosynthetic bacteria, and the pili are used for attachment and conjugation. The bacterial chromosome also carries essential genes, but the plasmid is the structure classically associated with nitrogen fixation in this syllabus. **Answer: C.**

**6.** Above which temperature do human enzymes begin to denature?

a) 37°C
b) 40°C
c) 45°C
d) 50°C

Human enzymes work best near body temperature (37 °C). Above about 40 °C the weak hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the tertiary structure begin to break, the active site loses its shape and the activity falls; by 50 to 60 °C most enzymes are completely and irreversibly denatured. 37 °C is the optimum, not a denaturing temperature, so the temperature above which denaturation begins is 40 °C. **Answer: B.**

**7.** The force that holds liquids in a continuous stream is called:

a) cohesion.
b) adhesion.
c) transpiration pull.
d) root pressure.

Cohesion is the attraction between molecules of the same substance. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules hold them together in an unbroken column (as in the xylem vessels), so the stream does not break. Adhesion is attraction between water and the walls of the vessel, transpiration pull is the suction created by evaporation from the leaves, and root pressure is a push from the roots. **Answer: A.**

**8.** Humans have three different types of pigments for carriage of oxygen. These pigments vary in their capacities to carry oxygen as depicted by the curves below.

Using these curves carefully identify the different pigments.

b) X = foetal haemoglobin; Y = myoglobin; Z = normal haemoglobin.
c) X = normal haemoglobin; Y = foetal .
d) haemoglobin; Z = myoglobin.

The three pigments differ in their affinity for oxygen. A curve shifted to the left reaches a given saturation at a lower partial pressure of oxygen, so it belongs to the pigment with the highest affinity. Myoglobin (in muscle) has the highest affinity of the three, foetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity than adult haemoglobin so that it can take oxygen from the mother's blood in the placenta, and normal (adult) haemoglobin has the lowest affinity, so its curve is farthest to the right. At the marked partial pressure (about 30 mm Hg) the curve X is about 70 % saturated, Y about 50 % and Z about 37 %. **9.** In a randomly breeding human population, one person out of 1000 is albino. Calculate the approximate frequency of heterozygous breeding individuals in this population.

*Options as printed:* A) 2%   B) 1%   C) 44%   D) 25%

Albinism is recessive, so albinos have the genotype $aa$ and the Hardy-Weinberg equation applies: $q^2 = 1/1000 = 0.001$, so $q = \sqrt{0.001} \approx 0.0316$ and $p = 1 - q \approx 0.9684$. The frequency of heterozygotes is $2pq = 2 \times 0.9684 \times 0.0316 \approx 0.0612$, about 6 %. This value is not among the printed options (2 %, 1 %, 44 %, 25 %); 2 % (option A) would be obtained if one person in 10 000 were albino ($q = 0.01$, $2pq \approx 0.0198$). The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**10.** Hydrolysis of lipid molecules will yield:

a) amino acids and glycerol.
b) fatty acids and glycerol.
c) glycerol and water.
d) glucose and water.

A triglyceride is made of one glycerol molecule joined by ester bonds to three fatty acids. Hydrolysis by lipase breaks the ester bonds and releases fatty acids and glycerol. Amino acids come from proteins and glucose from carbohydrates. **Answer: B.**

**11.** In angiosperms, double fertilization results in a diploid zygote and a:

a) triploid embryo.
b) diploid embryo.
c) triploid pericarp.
d) triploid endosperm.

One male gamete fuses with the egg cell ($n + n$) to form the diploid zygote, which becomes the embryo. The second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei of the embryo sac ($n + n + n$) to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into the endosperm that nourishes the embryo. The pericarp is formed from the ovary wall and is not a product of fertilization. **Answer: D.**

**12.** A transgenic organism is characterized by the presence of:

a) plasmid.
b) recombinant DNA.
c) recombinant RNA.
d) restriction endonuclease.

A transgenic organism has received a gene from another species. This foreign gene is spliced into its DNA as recombinant DNA (DNA made of sequences from two sources). A plasmid is only a vector, restriction endonuclease is the enzyme used to cut DNA, and recombinant RNA is not the criterion. **Answer: B.**

**13.** An example of convergent evolution is:

a) wings of insects and wings of birds.
b) wings of birds and pentadactyl limbs of the whales.
c) appendix of man and the caecum of rodents.
d) coccyx of man and the tail of a horse.

Convergent evolution gives similar (analogous) structures with the same function in unrelated groups under similar selection pressures. Insect wings (chitinous outgrowths) and bird wings (modified forelimbs) are analogous. The bird wing and the pentadactyl limb of whales, and the appendix of man and the caecum of rodents, are homologous structures, which show divergent evolution. The coccyx and the horse's tail are also homologous. **Answer: A.**

**14.** In the fruit fly, grey body is dominant over black body and long wing over vestigial wing. The genes controlling these characters are linked. | Phenotype | Number |
|---|---|
| grey body, long wing | 1000 |
| black body, vestigial wing | 800 |

| grey body, vestigial wing | 200 |

**15.** $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ in living organisms:

**16.** Which of the following is correct of glycolysis?

(i) It takes place in the mitochondrion.

(ii) It produces much of the ATP in tissue respiration.

(iii) It does not occur in bacterial cells.

(iv) It is the main process producing energy in yeast fermentation.

a) (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
b) (i) and (iii) are correct.
c) (ii) and (iv) are correct.
d) only (iv) is correct.

Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, so (i) is wrong. It gives a net gain of only 2 ATP per glucose, whereas most ATP in tissue (aerobic) respiration comes from oxidative phosphorylation, so (ii) is wrong. Bacteria also use glycolysis, so (iii) is wrong. In alcoholic fermentation the only ATP produced comes from glycolysis (the later steps only regenerate NAD), so (iv) is correct. **17.** Extinction of species can be prevented by:

(i) destroying the habitats.

(ii) not protecting the species.

(iii) increasing the use of bio-poisons.

a) (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
b) (i) and (iii) are correct.
c) (ii) and (iv) are correct.
d) only (iv) is correct.

Destroying habitats, leaving species unprotected and using more poisons all increase the risk of extinction. Controlling and reducing the harmful effects of modern agriculture (habitat clearing, pesticides, monoculture) helps to conserve species. Only (iv) is correct. **Answer: D.**

**18.** During the process of digestion in rodents:

(i) food is stored in the rumen.

(ii) upper incisors are absent.

(iii) the gizzard helps to grind food material.

(iv) mutualistic micro-organisms digest cellulose in the caecum.

a) (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
b) (i) and (iii) are correct.
c) (ii) and (iv) are correct.
d) only (iv) is correct.

The rumen belongs to ruminants (cattle, goats) and the absence of upper incisors (replaced by a horny pad) is also a ruminant feature, so (i) and (ii) are wrong. The gizzard is found in birds and earthworms, not in rodents, so (iii) is wrong. Rodents (and rabbits) have a large caecum in which symbiotic bacteria digest cellulose, so (iv) is correct. Only (iv) is correct. **Answer: D.**

**19.** The overall purpose of the Calvin cycle is to:

(i) generate molecules of ATP.

(ii) generate NADPH.

(iii) assist plants in tissue respiration.

(iv) build organic molecules.

a) (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
b) (i) and (iii) are correct.
c) (ii) and (iv) are correct.
d) only (iv) is correct.

The Calvin cycle (light-independent stage) uses the ATP and NADPH made in the light-dependent reactions to reduce carbon dioxide to triose phosphate and then to glucose and other organic molecules. It consumes ATP and NADPH, it does not generate them, and it has no role in respiration. Only (iv) is correct. **Answer: D.**

**20.** Kranz anatomy is:

(i) the biochemical pathway through which $\mathrm{C}_4$ plants carry out photosynthesis.

(ii) the arrangement of chloroplast-containing cells around the vascular bundles of the leaf.

(iii) a distinctive sheath of cells around the root hairs for absorption of water.

(iv) the arrangement of bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles of the leaf.

a) (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
b) (i) and (iii) are correct.
c) (ii) and (iv) are correct.
d) only (iv) is correct.

Kranz (wreath) anatomy is a structural feature of $\mathrm{C}_4$ leaves: the vascular bundles are surrounded by a ring of bundle sheath cells that contain chloroplasts, and the mesophyll cells are arranged in turn around this ring. (ii) and (iv) describe this arrangement. (i) describes the $\mathrm{C}_4$ pathway, not the anatomy, and (iii) has nothing to do with leaves. So (ii) and (iv) are correct. **Answer: C.**

**21.** The molar of a human:

(i) has 4 or 5 cusps.

(ii) is used for tearing flesh.

(iii) is used for grinding and crushing of food.

(iv) is the last to appear in the milk dentition of humans.

a) (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.
b) (i) and (iii) are correct.
c) (ii) and (iv) are correct.
d) only (iv) is correct.

A human molar is a broad tooth with 4 or 5 cusps (i), adapted for grinding and crushing food (iii). Tearing flesh is the work of the canines, so (ii) is wrong. The permanent molars have no predecessors and do not belong to the milk dentition (they appear after it, with the permanent teeth), so (iv) is wrong. Hence (i) and (iii) are correct. **Answer: B.**

**22.** The gametophyte in a moss, liverwort and fern:

a) is haploid.
b) is reduced.
c) is green and photosynthetic.
d) is anchored by unicellular rhizoids.

In all land plants the gametophyte is the haploid generation that makes the gametes by mitosis. In mosses and liverworts it is the dominant, green plant held to the soil by rhizoids; in ferns it is a small independent heart-shaped prothallus. What all three groups share is that the gametophyte is haploid. The sporophyte is the diploid generation; option B (reduced) fits only the gametophyte of seed plants, and C and D are not true of all three groups (the moss gametophyte has multicellular rhizoids). **Answer: A.**

**23.** According to the fluid mosaic model, a plasma membrane is composed of:

a) phospholipid and hemicellulose.
b) phospholipid and polysaccharide.
c) phospholipid, extrinsic and intrinsic proteins.
d) phospholipid and surface proteins.

In the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson) the membrane is a fluid bilayer of phospholipid in which protein molecules float like a mosaic: intrinsic (integral) proteins span the bilayer and extrinsic (peripheral) proteins lie on its surfaces. Hemicellulose and polysaccharides are not structural components of the plasma membrane. **Answer: C.**

**24.** When glomerular filtrate is produced in the kidney tubule, it moves from:

a) proximal convoluted tubule to distal convoluted tubule.
b) proximal convoluted tubule to collecting duct.
c) proximal convoluted tubule to loop of Henle.
d) distal convoluted tubule to proximal convoluted tubule.

The filtrate leaves the Bowman's capsule and enters the proximal convoluted tubule (where glucose, amino acids and most of the water and salts are reabsorbed), then flows down the loop of Henle, then into the distal convoluted tubule and finally the collecting duct. The only option giving the right order is: proximal convoluted tubule to loop of Henle. **Answer: C.**

**25.** Which of the following pairs of hormones work together so that sperms can be produced from spermatogonia?

a) LH and FSH
b) GnRh and FSH
c) LH and FSH
d) Testosterone and FSH

Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules needs two hormonal signals: FSH from the anterior pituitary, which acts on the Sertoli cells, and testosterone from the Leydig (interstitial) cells, which is produced under the control of LH (ICSH) and acts on the developing germ cells. So the pair that acts directly on the tubules is testosterone and FSH. LH alone only stimulates testosterone secretion and GnRH acts on the pituitary. (Options A and C are printed identically.) **Answer: D.**

**26.** How does the myelin sheath increase the speed of impulse transmission?

*Options as printed:* A) It restricts the potential difference to the Node of Ranvier.   B) It promotes a change in potential difference along an axon   C) It ensures that the ions are kept close to the axon membrane

The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer around the axon. Ions can cross the membrane only at the gaps in the sheath (the nodes of Ranvier), so the action potential (the change in potential difference) is restricted to the nodes and the impulse jumps from node to node by local circuits: this is saltatory conduction, which is much faster than the continuous spread along an unmyelinated axon. The answer expected is that the sheath restricts the depolarization to the nodes of Ranvier (the first printed option, A).

**Intended answer: A (It restricts the potential difference to the Node of Ranvier).**

b) RNA polymerase.
c) tRNA.
d) mRNA.

**29.** A body cavity completely surrounded by tissue derived from the mesoderm that provides cushioning for internal organs is called:

a) a coelom.
b) a pseudocoelom.
c) an archenteron.
d) a gastrovascular cavity.

A true coelom is a fluid-filled body cavity lined on all sides by mesoderm (the body wall and the gut are both covered by mesodermal tissue), which cushions and protects the organs. In a pseudocoelom the cavity is lined by mesoderm only on the outside, an archenteron is the primitive gut of the gastrula, and a gastrovascular cavity is the digestive and circulatory cavity of cnidarians. **Answer: A.**

**30.** Which of these organisms has the largest number of chambers in its heart?

a) Amphibian.
b) Reptile.
c) Bird.
d) Shark.

The shark has a two-chambered heart (one atrium and one ventricle), the amphibian has three chambers (two atria and one ventricle), and the typical reptile has three chambers (two atria and a partly divided ventricle). Birds, like mammals, have a four-chambered heart (two atria and two ventricles) which completely separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The bird has the largest number of chambers. **Answer: C.**

**First statement:** There are more males than females that suffer from haemophilia.

**Second statement:** The gene for haemophilia is found on the X chromosome.

a) Both statements are true and the second explains the first.
b) Both statements are true but the second does not explain the first.
c) The first statement is true and the second is false.
d) The first statement is false and the second is true.

Both statements are true. Haemophilia is a recessive sex-linked disease and the allele lies on the X chromosome. A male has only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele ($X^hY$) makes him haemophiliac, whereas a female must be homozygous recessive ($X^hX^h$) to show it, which is much rarer. The second statement therefore explains the first. **Answer: A.**

**First statement:** The cell surface membrane of all living cells carry a potential difference.

**Second statement:** The sodium / potassium pump continuously pumps $\mathrm{Na}^+$ out of the cell and $\mathrm{K}^+$ into the cell.

a) Both statements are true and the second explains the first.
b) Both statements are true but the second does not explain the first.
c) The first statement is true and the second is false.
d) The first statement is false and the second is true.

Both statements are true. Every living cell has a resting potential, with the inside negative relative to the outside. The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 $\mathrm{Na}^+$ out for 2 $\mathrm{K}^+$ in at the cost of ATP, so it builds up an unequal distribution of charge and ions across the membrane, which is the main cause of the potential difference. The second explains the first. **Answer: A.**

**First statement:** Meiosis produces haploid gametes in organisms.

**Second statement:** Meiosis is characterized by two consecutive divisions.

a) Both statements are true and the second explains the first.
b) Both statements are true but the second does not explain the first.
c) The first statement is true and the second is false.
d) The first statement is false and the second is true.

Both statements are true: in animals meiosis gives haploid gametes, and meiosis consists of two successive nuclear divisions (meiosis I and II) with a single replication of DNA. Having two divisions does not by itself explain why the products are haploid (the halving is due to the separation of homologous chromosomes in the first division), so the second statement does not explain the first. **Answer: B.**

Only about 10 % of the energy of one trophic level passes to the next (the rest is lost as heat in respiration, in excreta and in uneaten parts), so the energy available falls at each step and the energy pyramid is always upright, whereas pyramids of numbers or biomass can be inverted. The second statement explains the first. **Answer: A.**

**First statement:** Classification can be done based on the uses of the organisms e.g. medical values.

**Second statement:** This type of classification is known as the natural system of classification.

a) Both statements are true and the second explains the first.
b) Both statements are true but the second does not explain the first.
c) The first statement is true and the second is false.
d) The first statement is false and the second is true.

The first statement is true: organisms can be grouped by their uses (food, medicine, timber). The second is false: such a grouping is an artificial classification, because it uses one or a few convenient characters. The natural system groups organisms by overall similarity and evolutionary relationships. **Answer: C.**

**41.** In penicillin production, the fermentation process is described as:

a) Batch fermentation.
b) Continuous culture.
c) "Fed-batch" culture.
d) Downstream processing.

Penicillin is a secondary metabolite: it is made after the rapid growth phase of the fungus Penicillium, when the nutrients (the carbon source and the precursor) are added gradually to the fermenter and the product is harvested at the end. This is a 'fed-batch' culture. In a continuous culture the medium is continually added and removed (as for single-cell protein), and downstream processing is the recovery and purification of the product after fermentation. **Answer: C.**

**42.** Some bacteria can effectively carry out metabolism in the presence or absence of oxygen. They are described as:

a) aerobic.
b) anaerobic.
c) fermentative microbes.
d) facultative anaerobes.

Facultative anaerobes can respire aerobically when oxygen is available and switch to fermentation or anaerobic respiration when it is absent (e.g. Escherichia coli). Strict aerobes need oxygen, strict (obligate) anaerobes cannot grow in oxygen, and 'fermentative microbes' only describes a type of metabolism. **Answer: D.**

**43.** Which of the following processes produce the maximum energy yield when one molecule of glucose is oxidized?

a) Oxidative phosphorylation.
b) Oxidation of pyruvic acid.
c) Glycolysis in the mitochondria.
d) Glycolysis in the cytoplasm.

Per molecule of glucose, glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP, the Krebs cycle (including the oxidation of pyruvic acid) gives 2 ATP directly, and oxidative phosphorylation, in which the reduced NAD and FAD are reoxidized along the electron transport chain, gives about 26 to 28 of the 30 to 32 ATP formed. Oxidative phosphorylation therefore gives the maximum yield. **Answer: A.**

**44.** The enzyme cholinesterase which hydrolyses acetylcholine to choline acts on the:

a) postsynaptic membrane.
b) presynaptic membrane.
c) synaptic cleft.
d) neuromuscular junction.

After acetylcholine has crossed the synaptic cleft and stimulated the receptors, cholinesterase breaks it down to choline and ethanoic (acetic) acid in the synaptic cleft, so that the post-synaptic membrane is not stimulated continuously. **46.** A male with underdeveloped testes, breast development, subnormal intelligence and an abnormal karyotype is likely to have:

b) Down's syndrome.
c) Turner's syndrome.
d) Huntington disease.

Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY, 47 chromosomes) gives a sterile male with small testes, some breast development (gynaecomastia), a tall body and often reduced intelligence. **47.** Which of the following tends to produce more organic material than it uses?

*Options as printed:* A) The shrub community.   B) The herb community.   C) The pine community.   D) The dense shrub community.

A community produces more organic material than it uses (production greater than community respiration, so that the P/R ratio is above 1) while it is still developing and biomass is accumulating. In an ecological succession the early communities have a high ratio of production to respiration, whereas the climax (such as a pine forest, with a large biomass to maintain) has a P/R ratio close to 1. Among the printed options the herb community, a young seral stage with rapid growth and little standing biomass to respire, is the intended answer, but shrub communities that are still closing their canopy also have P/R above 1, so the printed options do not give one unambiguous choice.

**48.** The solute potential of cells kept in pure water for two days is $-900$ kPa. The pressure potential of these cells is:

a) $-1800$ kPa
b) $1800$ kPa
c) $900$ kPa
d) $-900$ kPa

Cells kept in pure water until equilibrium is reached are fully turgid and have the same water potential as pure water: $\psi = 0$. Since $\psi = \psi_s + \psi_p$, the pressure potential is $\psi_p = \psi - \psi_s = 0 - (-900) = +900$ kPa. The pressure potential of a turgid cell is positive and equal in size to the solute potential. **Answer: C.**

**49.** The presence of a perivisceral cavity in the mesoderm of triploblastic multicellular organisms makes them to be called:

a) acoelomates.
b) pseudocoelomates.
c) coelomates.
d) coelenterates.

A perivisceral cavity (body cavity around the viscera) that is formed within the mesoderm and lined by it is a true coelom, and animals that have it are coelomates (annelids, molluscs, arthropods, vertebrates). Acoelomates have no body cavity, pseudocoelomates have a cavity not completely lined by mesoderm, and coelenterates are diploblastic. **Answer: C.**

**50.** Reverse transcriptase is used in genetic engineering do which of the following?

a) Synthesize the desired gene artificially.
b) Chop DNA into pieces and search for the desired gene.
c) Extract a copy of the gene from DNA.
d) Make a copy of the gene from its mRNA.

Reverse transcriptase is the enzyme of retroviruses that makes DNA from an RNA template. In genetic engineering it is used to make a copy of a gene (complementary DNA, cDNA) from its mRNA, which is easily isolated from the cells where the gene is active. The cDNA, which has no introns, can then be inserted into a plasmid vector and expressed in bacteria. **Answer: D.**

**1.** The number of moles of carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_2}$) gas present in $44.8\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ at standard temperature and pressure (STP) (molar gas volume $= 22\,400\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) is given by:

b) $44.0\ \mathrm{cm^3} / 22\,400\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}$
c) $44.0\ \mathrm{cm^3} / 44.8\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}$
d) $(44.8\ \mathrm{cm^3} \times 44\ \mathrm{cm^3}) / 22\,400\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}$

Amount of gas $=$ volume of gas $\div$ molar gas volume. Here $n = \dfrac{44.8\ \mathrm{cm^3}}{22\,400\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}} = 0.002\ \mathrm{mol}$. **2.** When the nuclide $^{239}_{93}\mathrm{Np}$ undergoes beta decay ($\beta^-$ decay) the nuclide produced is

a) $^{239}_{92}\mathrm{U}$
b) $^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}$
c) $^{239}_{94}\mathrm{Pa}$ (as printed)
d) $^{240}_{93}\mathrm{Np}$

In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron becomes a proton: the mass number stays the same ($239$) and the atomic number rises by one ($93 \rightarrow 94$): $^{239}_{93}\mathrm{Np} \rightarrow {}^{239}_{94}\mathrm{X} + {}^{0}_{-1}e + \bar\nu$. Element 94 is plutonium (Pu), so the product is $^{239}_{94}\mathrm{Pu}$. Option C is the only one with mass number $239$ and atomic number $94$; its symbol is printed 'Pa' (protactinium is $Z = 91$), which is a misprint for Pu. A and B have $Z = 92$, D has $Z = 93$ and a different mass number. **Answer: C.**

**3.** The relative molecular mass of a hydrocarbon is 56. What is its molecular formula?

a) $\mathrm{C_4H_8}$
b) $\mathrm{C_3H_6}$
c) $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$
d) $\mathrm{C_3H_8}$

$M_r(\mathrm{C_4H_8}) = 4(12) + 8(1) = 56$. The others give $\mathrm{C_3H_6} = 42$, $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}} = 58$, $\mathrm{C_3H_8} = 44$. **Answer: A.**

**4.** In a nitrate(V), $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$,

a) The nitrogen reacting atom uses 5 unpaired electrons for bonding.
b) Nitrogen forms one dative bond and three covalent bonds.
c) Nitrogen promotes one 2s electron to a higher energy level.
d) Nitrogen readily loses five electrons.

Nitrogen ($2s^2 2p^3$) has only three unpaired electrons, so A is wrong; there is no $2d$ level for promotion (C), and N does not form $\mathrm{N^{5+}}$ (D). In the nitrate ion nitrogen uses its three unpaired electrons for covalent bonds (one double bond to one oxygen counts as two, one single bond to $\mathrm{O^-}$ as one) and its lone pair forms a dative bond to the third oxygen: one dative bond and three covalent bonds. **Answer: B.**

b) 3,3-dimethylbutane

d) $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^3\,4s^2$

**7.** Given that the standard enthalpies of formation in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ of $\mathrm{CO(g)}$, $\mathrm{CO_2(g)}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$ are respectively $-110$, $-394$ and $-242$. **14.** When the compound represented by the structural formula $\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}O{-}CHO}$ (phenyl methanoate: a benzene ring bonded to $\mathrm{O{-}C(=O){-}H}$) is warmed with aqueous solution of dilute sodium hydroxide, the most likely products formed are

**15.** The two nuclei in the hydrogen molecule ion ($\mathrm{H_2^+}$) are held together by

a) an ionic bond.
b) a dative covalent bond.
c) electrostatic attraction between the two hydrogen atoms.
d) mutual sharing of the electron charge cloud.

$\mathrm{H_2^+}$ contains two protons and one electron. The two nuclei repel each other; they are held together because the single electron's charge cloud lies between them and attracts both nuclei: this is a (one-electron) covalent bond, i.e. mutual sharing of the electron charge cloud. There are no ions of opposite charge (A), and C is wrong because the nuclei are not attracted to each other. **Answer: D.**

**16.** The acidity constant of propanoic acid is $1.26 \times 10^{-5}$. What is the pH of a $0.1\ \mathrm{M}$ solution of this acid?

b) 1.12

**19.** Two pure liquids, S and T, which form an ideal mixture, have vapour pressures $12.9\ \mathrm{kPa}$ and $26.8\ \mathrm{kPa}$ respectively at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is the vapour pressure of a mixture containing $2.0$ moles of S and $1.0$ mole of T and $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

**23.** One property of a buffer solution, prepared from a weak acid and its sodium salt is that

a) its pH is less than the pH of the original acid
b) its pH is unaffected by the addition of any quantity of $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions
c) its pH is greater than the pH of the original acid

b) All the tetrachlorides hydrolyze in water to give acidic solutions
c) PbO is amphoteric while $\mathrm{PbO_2}$ is acidic

**1.** A foreigner can acquire Cameroonian citizenship by ...

a) Naturalisation
b) Birth
c) Settlement
d) Nationalization

A foreigner who meets the conditions set by law (for example a period of residence in the country) and applies for it can be granted Cameroonian nationality. This legal procedure is called **naturalisation**. Birth gives nationality to a child (by descent or by place of birth), not to a foreigner. Settlement (simply living in the country) does not by itself give citizenship, and nationalization is the taking over of private property by the State, a different idea that only looks like the word naturalisation.

**Answer: A.**

**1.** A three input NOR gate gives a logic high output only when:

a) One input is high
b) One input is low
c) Two input are low
d) All input are low.

A NOR gate is an OR gate followed by a NOT gate: $Y = \overline{A + B + C}$. The OR part is 0 only when all three inputs are 0, so the output is 1 only when **all inputs are low**. With one or two inputs high, the OR part is 1 and the NOR output is 0.

**2.** The binary form of $77.25_{10}$ is:

a) 1001101.01
b) 1001101.001
c) 10110010.10
d) 10110010.11

Integer part: $77 = 64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 1001101_2$. Fractional part: $0.25 = \tfrac14 = 0.01_2$ (0.25 x 2 = 0.5 gives 0, 0.5 x 2 = 1.0 gives 1). So $77.25_{10} = 1001101.01_2$. Options C and D start with 10110010, which is 178, not 77.

**3.** In memory hierarchy, the larger the memory the:

a) Higher the access time and the higher the speed of transfer of data to CPU
b) Higher the access time and the lower the speed of transfer of data to CPU
c) Shorter the access time and the higher the speed of transfer of data to CPU
d) Shorter the access time and the lower the speed of transfer of data to CPU.

Down the memory hierarchy (registers, cache, main memory, disk) capacity increases while cost per bit falls, but the access time gets longer and the transfer rate to the CPU gets lower. So a larger memory has a **higher access time and a lower speed of transfer**. Options A, C and D contradict this trade-off. **Answer: B.**

**4.** Dynamic RAM, as opposed to Static RAM, is generally used as main memory in a computer system because it:

a) consumes acceptable power
b) has higher speed
c) has lower cell density
d) needs refreshing in circuitry.

DRAM stores a bit in one transistor and one capacitor, so it has a **higher** cell density, a lower cost per bit and a lower power consumption than SRAM (six transistors per cell); this is why it is used for the large main memory. Option B is false (SRAM is faster), option C is false (DRAM has the higher density) and option D (refreshing) is a drawback, not a reason for the choice. The only advantage listed is the acceptable power consumption. **Answer: A.**

**5.** $-27_{10}$ can be represented in a signed magnitude format and in a 1's complement format as:

a) 111011 & 100100
b) 100100 & 111011
c) 011011 & 100100
d) 100100 & 011011.

$27 = 011011_2$ on 6 bits. Signed magnitude: set the sign bit to 1 and keep the magnitude bits, giving $111011$. 1's complement: invert every bit of $011011$, giving $100100$. So the pair is $111011$ and $100100$. Option B swaps the two formats; options C and D keep a positive sign bit for the signed-magnitude form. **Answer: A.**

**9.** The equivalence of the Boolean expression $z = x(\bar{x} + \bar{y})$ is:

*Options as printed:* A) $z = x(xy)$   B) $z = \bar{x}\, y$   C) $z = x\, \bar{y}$   D) $z = x\,(\overline{xy})$

Distribute: $x(\bar{x} + \bar{y}) = x\bar{x} + x\bar{y} = 0 + x\bar{y} = x\bar{y}$. A truth-table check over the four values of $(x, y)$ confirms $x\bar{y}$ (true only for $x=1, y=0$). Option C is therefore equivalent. Option D, $x\,\overline{xy}$, is also equivalent, because by De Morgan $\overline{xy} = \bar{x} + \bar{y}$, so it is the original expression rewritten; options A ($xy$) and B ($\bar{x}y$) are not equivalent.

**Intended answer: C ($x\bar{y}$, the simplified form), but D is also equivalent by De Morgan.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**10.** The circuit used to memorize one bit of data is known as a/an:

a) Register
b) Encoder
c) Cell
d) Flip-Flop.

A **flip-flop** is the bistable circuit that stores one bit (built from gates with feedback). A register is a group of flip-flops (several bits), an encoder is a combinational circuit with no memory, and 'cell' is a generic word for a storage location. **Answer: D.**

**11.** What is the characteristic of the RAM that makes it suitable to manage processes in memory?

*Options as printed:* A) It is volatile   B) It is small in size   C) Its access is direct   D) Its information can be overwritten.

RAM (random access memory) lets the system reach any location directly in the same time, and its contents can be read and written freely, so a process image can be loaded, run and modified at any address. Volatility (A) and small size (B) are not advantages for process management. Both C (direct/random access) and D (can be overwritten) are true properties of RAM and the question does not say which one is meant.

**Intended answer: C (its access is direct), although D (its contents can be overwritten) is also a valid property.**

**12.** Memory management is necessary because:

a) The memory is finite
b) Many programs have to run simultaneously
c) Free memory space has to be relocated
d) All of the above.

Main memory is limited (A), several programs must share it at the same time (B), and free space has to be allocated, reclaimed and relocated as processes come and go (C). All three statements justify memory management, so the correct option is 'All of the above'. **Answer: D.**

**13.** The Shortest Job First is a process scheduling strategy which is:

*Options as printed:* A) Pre-emptive   B) Non-pre-emptive   C) Free memory space has to be reallocated   D) Suitable in batch processing.

SJF selects the waiting process with the shortest next CPU burst. In its basic form the chosen process runs to completion, so it is non-pre-emptive; its pre-emptive variant is called Shortest Remaining Time First. SJF is also well suited to batch systems, where job lengths are known in advance, so options B and D are both defensible, and A holds for the pre-emptive variant. Option C is unrelated (memory management).

**Intended answer: B (non-pre-emptive, the basic form of SJF); D (suitable for batch processing) is also true.**

**14.** Analysis which determines the meaning of a statement once its grammatical structure is correct is known as:

a) Syntactic analysis
b) Semantic analysis
c) Grammatical analysis
d) Lexical analysis.

In a compiler, lexical analysis splits the text into tokens, syntactic analysis (parsing) checks the grammatical structure, and **semantic analysis** then checks the meaning (types, declared variables, valid operations) of statements that are already grammatically correct. 'Grammatical analysis' is another word for syntax checking. **Answer: B.**

**15.** A technique that allows for the execution of a program that is not entirely in memory is known as:

a) Demand paging
b) Fixed partitioning
c) Swapping
d) Pooling.

**Demand paging** is the virtual-memory technique that loads a page into main memory only when it is referenced, so a program can run while only part of it is resident. Fixed partitioning needs the whole program in a partition, swapping moves whole processes in and out, and pooling is not a memory technique. **Answer: A.**

**16.** The scheduling algorithm in which the CPU is allocated to the process with the least CPU-burst time is called:

a) Priority scheduling
b) Round Robin
c) Shortest Job First
d) First-Come-First-Served.

Allocating the CPU to the process whose next CPU burst is the smallest is the definition of **Shortest Job First**. Priority scheduling uses a priority number, Round Robin uses a time quantum and FCFS uses arrival order. **Answer: C.**

**17.** It is not a direct or indirect advantage of distributed systems.

a) Resource sharing
b) Reliability
c) Incremental growth
d) None of the above.

Resource sharing, reliability (the system survives the failure of one node) and incremental growth (nodes can be added step by step) are all classical advantages of distributed systems. Since A, B and C are advantages, none of them is the exception, and the correct choice is 'None of the above'. **Answer: D.**

**18.** Nested sub-program call-returns are invoked using a:

a) First-in-First-out approach
b) Round Robin approach
c) Last in first out approach
d) Last in last out approach.

The last subprogram called is the first one to finish and return, so the call chain is handled by a stack, which is a **last-in first-out** structure. A FIFO queue would return to the first caller first, which is wrong. **Answer: C.**

**19.** Which of the following is NOT characteristic of a relational database model?

a) Tables
b) Tree like structure
c) Complex logical relationships
d) None of the above.

A relational database stores data in tables (relations) linked by keys. A tree-like (parent-child) structure belongs to the **hierarchical** model, so it is not characteristic of the relational model. Option C (complex logical relationships, obtained by joins) is used to describe the relational model's flexibility. **Answer: B.**

**20.** A program parameter that can be modified by all subprograms that make reference to it is known as a/an:

a) Local variable
b) Global variable
c) Formal parameter
d) Actual parameter.

A **global variable** is visible to every subprogram that refers to it, so any of them can modify it. A local variable exists only inside one subprogram; formal and actual parameters are the names in the definition and the values in the call and belong to one call. **Answer: B.**

**21.** Given the algorithmic statements below

```
If (A > N) or (B < 0), then
    A <- A + 1
    B <- B - 1
Else
    A <- B + N
Endif
```

The statement $A \leftarrow B + N$ is only executed:

*Options as printed:* A) When $A \ge N$ or $B \le 0$   B) When $A \ge N$ or $B < 0$   C) When $A \ge N$ and $B \le 0$   D) When $A \ge N$ A and $B < 0$.

The Else branch runs when the condition is false, that is $
eg\big((A > N) \lor (B < 0)\big) = (A \le N) \land (B \ge 0)$ by De Morgan. A brute-force check over small values of A, N and B confirms this. None of the printed options is this condition: they all use $A \ge N$, while the correct inequality is $A \le N$, and C uses $B \le 0$ instead of $B \ge 0$. Option C ('and') is the only one with the right logical structure, so the printed inequalities are probably reversed by a printing error.

**Intended answer: $A \le N$ and $B \ge 0$ (not exactly printed in any option; C has the right structure but with both inequalities reversed).**

**22.** If a software piece can be used either alone or together with other software pieces to produce a more sophisticated software, the software piece is said to be:

a) Adaptable
b) Manageable
c) Reusable
d) Predictable

A component that can be used on its own or combined with others in new, more complex software is **reusable**. Adaptable means easily modified, manageable means easy to control and predictable means its behaviour can be foreseen. **Answer: C.**

**23.** The popular expression "Divide-And-Conquer" refers to a kind of:

a) Top-down design
b) Object oriented design
c) Algorithmic design
d) Modular design

Divide-and-conquer is a classical **algorithm design** paradigm: split a problem into smaller sub-problems of the same kind, solve them (usually recursively) and combine the results (merge sort, quick sort, binary search). Top-down and modular design are system-design methods that also decompose problems, and object-oriented design is a different paradigm. **Answer: C.**

**24.** A software is said to be portable if:

a) It can be put on a CD-ROM
b) It can be installed in any computer
c) It is installable on more than one computer
d) It is platform independent

Portability means the software can run on different hardware or operating-system platforms with little or no change, that is, it is **platform independent**. Being stored on a CD-ROM (A) says nothing about this, and A software that installs on several machines of the same platform (C) is not necessarily portable. **Answer: D.**

**25.** What data structure will you most likely see in a non-recursive implementation of a recursive algorithm?

a) A stack
b) An array
c) A record
d) Queue

A recursive algorithm relies on the call stack to keep the parameters, local variables and return addresses of pending calls. To remove the recursion, the programmer simulates this behaviour with an explicit **stack** (last-in first-out). **Answer: A.**

**26.** A search technique for direct item access is:

a) Binary search
b) Linear search
c) Binary tree search
d) Hash table search

A hash function turns the key into the address of the item, so the item is reached directly (expected time $O(1)$) without comparing it with other items. Linear search scans item by item, and binary and binary-tree search halve the candidates at each comparison. **Answer: D.**

**27.** The smallest element of an array's index is called its:

a) Lower bound
b) Upper bound
c) Range
d) Limit.

The smallest valid index of an array is its **lower bound** (for example 0 in C, 1 in many Pascal arrays); the largest is the upper bound, and the range is the set (or number) of valid indices. **Answer: A.**

**28.** The Worst case occurs in linear search algorithms when an item is:

a) Somewhere in the middle of the array
b) Not in the array at all
c) The last element in the array
d) The last element in the array or is absent.

Linear search compares the item with every element in turn. The maximum number of comparisons ($n$) is needed when the item is the last element and also when it is absent, because the whole array is scanned in both cases. Options B and C each give only one of the two situations, so D is the complete answer. **Answer: D.**

**29.** One of the following is a recursive definition of the Fibonacci series.

a) $\begin{cases} f_0 = 0 \\ f_1 = 1 \\ f_n = f_{n-1} + f_{n-2} \end{cases}$
b) $\begin{cases} f_0 = 0 \\ f_1 = 1 \\ f_n = n * f_{n-2} \end{cases}$
c) $\begin{cases} f_n \leftarrow 1 \\ \textit{for } x \leftarrow 1 \textit{ to } n \textit{ do} \\ \quad f_n \leftarrow f_n * x \end{cases}$
d) None of the above

A recursive definition needs base cases and a rule that refers to smaller values of the same function. Option A gives the base cases $f_0 = 0$, $f_1 = 1$ and the rule $f_n = f_{n-1} + f_{n-2}$, which generates 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... Option B uses a wrong rule ($n \cdot f_{n-2}$), and option C is an iterative loop computing the factorial. **Answer: A.**

**30.** Which of these sort algorithms divides, at each iteration, the list into two sub-lists so that one is sorted and the other unsorted?

*Options as printed:* A) Quick sort   B) Insertion sort   C) Bubble sort   D) Merge sort

Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix and an unsorted remainder, and moves one element of the remainder into place at each iteration. Quick sort and merge sort split the list into two parts that are both still unsorted (quick sort around a pivot, merge sort in halves). Bubble sort also leaves a sorted tail after each pass, so it fits the description loosely.

**Intended answer: B (insertion sort); bubble sort (C) also leaves a sorted part and an unsorted part after each pass.**

**31.** When a subroutine is called, the address of the instruction following the CALL instruction is stored in/on the:

a) Stack pointer
b) Accumulator
c) Program counter
d) Stack

On CALL, the processor pushes the return address (the address of the next instruction) onto the **stack**, so that RETURN can pop it and resume there, and nested calls are handled in last-in first-out order. The stack pointer only holds the address of the top of the stack, the accumulator holds data, and the program counter is loaded with the subroutine's address (its old value is what is saved). **Answer: D.**

**32.** In object-oriented programming, an object is:

a) One instance of a class
b) Another word for a class
c) A class with static method
d) A method that accesses a class.

A class is the template (attributes and methods); an **object is one instance** created from that template, with its own state. **Answer: A.**

**33.** In general a low level language program:

a) Makes more system calls than a high level language program
b) Makes use of stacks quite often
c) Has more lines of code for same program than a high level language
d) Gives more accurate results than high level language.

A statement of a high-level language is translated into several machine or assembly instructions, so the same task needs **more lines of code** in a low-level language. System calls, stack use and accuracy do not depend on the level of the language. **Answer: C.**

**34.** In computability theory, a problem is said to be computable if:

*Options as printed:* A) Any kind of solution can be found   B) The problem is a mathematical problem   C) The problem has a feasible solution   D) The problem is a classical computing problem.

In computability theory a problem is computable (decidable or solvable) if there exists an algorithm, that is, a finite sequence of well-defined steps, that produces the solution for every input in finite time. None of the printed options states this exactly: A ('any kind of solution can be found') is vague, B and D describe the type of problem, and C ('feasible solution') is the nearest idea but 'feasible' normally refers to practicality.

**Intended answer: an algorithm exists that solves the problem in a finite number of steps; the nearest printed option is C (a feasible solution exists), but A is also loosely defensible.**

**35.** When implementing recursive programs we use:

a) An implicit program stack.
b) A programmer-managed stack
c) No program stack
d) Queues.

When a function calls itself, the language run-time automatically pushes a new activation record (parameters, local variables, return address) on the **implicit program (call) stack**; the programmer does not manage it. A programmer-managed stack is used only when the recursion is removed by hand. **Answer: A.**

**36.** Prototype refinement is:

a) Giving a prototype enough functionality such that it becomes the final product
b) Improving a prototype's functionality so that they are closer to the final product
c) Eliminating errors from a conceptual model
d) Developing a logical model from a conceptual one.

Refinement is the iterative step in which the prototype is improved and extended after user feedback so that it gets **closer to the final product**. Option A describes evolutionary prototyping, where the prototype itself becomes the product; C and D concern database or conceptual modelling. **Answer: B.**

**37.** In a mesh network topology:

a) A computer is connected to all other computers via the internet
b) A computer is connected to all other computers with the help of switches
c) A computer is connected to all other computers directly
d) A computer is connected to all other computers via other computers.

In a (full) mesh topology every node has its own **direct** link to each of the other nodes, which gives several paths and high reliability. Using the internet, switches or intermediate computers describes other designs (a partial mesh relays through other nodes). **Answer: C.**

**38.** Any system generally used for real time applications is known as:

a) An online information system
b) An information system
c) An information retrieval system
d) An embedded system.

Real-time applications (engine control, medical devices, appliances) run on **embedded systems**, computers built into a device and designed to respond within strict time limits. Information systems and information retrieval systems manage data for users and are not defined by real-time response. **Answer: D.**

**39.** It is NOT a measure for data security:

a) Locking up work premises after work
b) Introducing logins and passwords
c) Storing data in many places and copies
d) Updating a database regularly.

Locking premises is physical access control, logins and passwords are logical access control, and storing copies in several places is backup protection against loss. **Updating a database regularly** keeps the data current, but it does not protect it against loss, theft or unauthorised access, so it is not a security measure. **Answer: D.**

**40.** It is a computer crime to:

a) Publish someone else's picture on the internet
b) Copy someone else's publication
c) Open a pornographic website
d) Copy copyrighted material.

Copying copyrighted material (software, music, films, texts) without permission is **software and content piracy**, a classical computer crime. Publishing a picture or copying a publication is only an offence under certain conditions (consent, copyright) and visiting a website is not by itself a crime, so D is the most direct answer. **Answer: D.**

**41.** Viruses are an issue of network:

a) Reliability
b) Feasibility
c) Security
d) Performance.

**42.** The number of connections in a full mesh topology that has $n$ devices is given by:

a) $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$
b) $\dfrac{(n+1)(n-1)}{2}$
c) $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$
d) $\dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}$

Each of the $n$ devices is linked to the other $n - 1$, which counts every link twice, so the number of links is $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$. Check with $n = 5$: $5 \times 4 / 2 = 10$ links, whereas B gives 12, C gives 15 and D gives 6. **Answer: A.**

**43.** The main function of a browser is to:

a) Compile HTML
b) Interpret HTML
c) Decompile HTML
d) Transfer HTML.

A web browser fetches an HTML document and **interprets** it, that is, reads the markup and displays (renders) the page. HTML is not compiled to machine code or decompiled, and the transfer of pages is done by the HTTP protocol, not by the browser's display function. **Answer: B.**

**44.** The concept by which we apply existing operations to new data types is:

a) Inheritance
b) Polymorphism
c) Encapsulation
d) Prototyping.

**Polymorphism** lets the same operation (for example `+` or `print`) work on different or new data types, each type supplying its own behaviour. Inheritance reuses the attributes and methods of a parent class, encapsulation hides the data inside the object, and prototyping is a software development method. **Answer: B.**

**45.** If the state of a database no longer reflects a real life state the database is supposed to capture, then such a database state is said to be:

a) Consistent
b) Durable
c) Parallel
d) Inconsistent.

A database state that does not match the real-world situation it models (or violates its integrity constraints) is **inconsistent**. A consistent state is the opposite; durability concerns data surviving failures and 'parallel' is not a database-state property. **Answer: D.**

**46.** Recursive algorithms use a:

a) Divide-and-conquer approach
b) Modular approach
c) Structural approach
d) Hierarchical approach.

A recursive algorithm solves a problem by reducing it to smaller instances of the same problem and combining the results, which is the **divide-and-conquer** approach. **Answer: A.**

**47.** The benefit of prototyping is:

a) Missing functions of the user can be identified
b) Misunderstanding between software developer and user can be identified
c) Incomplete or inconsistent user requirements may be detected.
d) All of the above.

Showing the user a working model early reveals functions the user forgot to mention (A), misunderstandings between developer and user (B), and incomplete or inconsistent requirements (C). All three are benefits, so the answer is 'All of the above'. **Answer: D.**

**48.** A database table is in $3^{rd}$ normal form if:

a) It is in $2^{nd}$ normal form (2NF) and in $1^{st}$ normal form (1NF)
b) It is in 2NF and all non-key fields depend on all key fields
c) It is in 2NF and all non-key fields depend only on the key
d) It is in 2NF and all non-key fields may depend indirectly on all key fields.

A table is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute: every non-key field depends **only on the key** (no transitive dependency). Option A only describes 2NF (and 1NF), option B repeats the 2NF requirement (full dependence on the whole key), and option D allows indirect (transitive) dependence, which 3NF forbids. **Answer: C.**

**49.** Given the relations CLASS(ClassID, Cycle, Teachinghours) and STUDENT(StudentID, ClassID, StudName). What is the possible relation between STUDENT and CLASS?

a) A class must have at least a student.
b) A student must have a class
c) A student may have no class
d) A class may have no students.

ClassID in STUDENT is a foreign key referring to CLASS: one class can be referred to by many students (one-to-many). Because a CLASS row exists independently of the STUDENT rows, nothing forces a class to have a student, so a **class may have no students**. Nothing in the schema forces a class to contain a student (A), and whether a student's ClassID may be empty (B, C) is not shown by the schema. **Answer: D.**

**50.** When requirements analysis goes wrong, what could happen?

a) The system may cost more than projected.
b) The system will become unreliable
c) The system may not meet user requirements
d) All of the above.

Errors in requirements analysis lead to rework (higher cost), to a system that misbehaves (unreliable) and to a product that does not do what users need. All three consequences can occur, so the answer is 'All of the above'. **Answer: D.**

The first generation of computers (1940s to mid 1950s) was built with valves (vacuum tubes). The second generation used transistors, the third used integrated circuits and the fourth used microprocessors. **Answer: A.**

**2.** Which is the odd one out below?

a) Monitor
b) Compiler
c) Keyboard
d) Printer

Monitor, keyboard and printer are all hardware devices connected to the computer. A compiler is a piece of software (a translator that converts a high-level program into machine code), so it is the odd one out. **Answer: B.**

**3.** Given that a computer uses one byte to represent a character, how many bits are used to represent 20 characters?

a) 160
b) 20
c) 1600
d) 200

One byte is 8 bits, so 20 characters need $20 \times 8 = 160$ bits. Option B counts characters (or bytes), not bits, and the others are wrong powers of ten. **Answer: A.**
