The universal donor is group O: its red cells carry neither antigen A nor antigen B, so they can be given to recipients of any group. Donor group O is the last row (D), which has the most ticks. In the printed table the cross for donor O to recipient A is a printing slip, because group O can be given to group A, but D is still the right choice: donor AB (A) can give only to AB, donor B (B) only to B and AB, donor A (C) only to A and AB. **Answer: D.**
In testing a leaf for the presence of starch, it is detached and placed in boiling water. What is the importance of this?

Boiling water kills the leaf, stops the chemical reactions in it and breaks down the cell membranes, so the cells become permeable and the iodine solution can reach the starch grains. The chlorophyll is removed later with hot ethanol (C, D), and the starch is not cooked on purpose (B). **Answer: A.**
To make the leaf cells more permeable to iodine.
To make the leaf cells transparent for easy colour change.
One reason why houses in the temperate regions have high pitched roofs is:

In temperate regions snow falls in winter. A steep roof lets the snow slide off, so that its weight does not build up and damage the roof. A snow blanket (C) would only add weight, and beauty (A) or direct heating (B) are not the reason. **Answer: D.**
to allow direct heating by the sun.
to allow snow to slide down easily.
What is the underlying principle of salting as a method of food preservation?

Salt draws water out of the food and out of the bacteria and fungi on it by osmosis. The food becomes dehydrated and the microorganisms cannot grow. Taste (B) is only a side effect, and salting does not destroy enzymes (C) or tenderise the food (D). **Answer: A.**
Which of the following will lead to inadequate ossification of bones?

Ossification is the hardening of bone by deposition of calcium phosphate. Vitamin D is needed for the absorption of calcium from the gut, so a lack of calcium and vitamin D gives soft, weak bones (rickets in children). Potassium, iron and vitamin K (A, C, D) are not needed for bone hardening in this way. **Answer: B.**
Deficiency in calcium and vitamin D.
Deficiency in calcium and vitamin K.
Select the appropriate cause and correction of long sightedness:

A long-sighted person sees distant objects clearly but not near ones. The eyeball is too short (or the lens too weak), so the image of a near object would form behind the retina. A converging (convex) lens adds the missing focusing power and corrects it. A long eyeball with a diverging lens (D) corrects short sightedness. **Answer: A.**
Small or short eye ball - converging lens.
Long or large eye ball - converging lens.
Small or short eye ball - diverging lens.
Long or large eye ball - diverging lens.
The part of the human ear which contains the organ of hearing is:

The cochlea, in the inner ear, contains the sensory cells that change sound vibrations into nerve impulses. The semicircular canals are for balance (A), the tympanum is the ear drum (B) and the eustachian tube equalises air pressure (C). **Answer: D.**

For questions 20 and 21, one or more of the statements are correct. Decide which of the statement(s) is/are correct, and then choose:
A - If [i], [ii] and [iii] are all correct.
B - If [i] and [ii] only are correct.
C - If [ii] and [iii] only are correct.
D - If [i] only is correct.

Pepsinogen is:

[i] Activated by hydrochloric acid.
[ii] Produced in an inactive form.
[iii] A blood clotting agent.

[i] is true: pepsinogen is changed into the active enzyme pepsin by hydrochloric acid in the stomach. [ii] is true: pepsinogen is the inactive form, which protects the stomach cells from being digested. [iii] is false: blood clotting agents are, for example, thrombin and fibrinogen. So only [i] and [ii] are correct. **Answer: B.**

In large scale water purification,

[i] Chlorination takes place in domestic reservoirs.
[ii] Addition of Flourine to the water prevents dental caries.
[iii] Water storage tanks must be covered.

[i] is false: in large scale purification the chlorine is added at the treatment works, after sedimentation and filtration, not in the reservoirs of homes. [ii] is true: fluoride added to the water helps to prevent tooth decay (dental caries). [iii] is true: covered tanks keep out dirt, animals and mosquitoes. So only [ii] and [iii] are correct. **Answer: C.**

$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \longrightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + 2880\ kJ}$ energy.

What amount of energy will be produced by the complete oxidation of 5 moles of glucose?
One mole of glucose releases 2880 kJ, so 5 moles release $5 \times 2880 = 14\,400$ kJ. A common slip is to divide or to move the decimal point wrongly (A, B, C). **Answer: D.**
The blood vessel which supplies oxygenated blood at high pressure to tissues and organs of the body is:

The aorta leaves the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood at high pressure to the body. The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood but only from the lungs to the heart, at low pressure (A); the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood (B); the vena cava brings deoxygenated blood back to the heart (D). **Answer: C.**

Which of these organs in the human body receives a double blood supply?

*Options as printed:* A) Kidney   B) Heart   C) Spleen   D) Brain

The organs usually quoted as having a double blood supply are the liver (hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein) and the lungs. None of them is among the options. Each organ listed has its own arterial supply (renal artery, coronary arteries, splenic artery, carotid and vertebral arteries), so the printed question cannot be marked automatically.

**Intended answer: the liver (hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein), which is not offered among the options.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
Select the compound epithelium from the list of tissues given below:

A compound (stratified) epithelium is made of several layers of cells. Transitional epithelium, which lines the bladder and can stretch, is a stratified epithelium. Columnar, squamous and ciliated cuboidal epithelia, as listed, are simple epithelia with a single layer of cells. **Answer: A.**

Study the food chain below:

algae → mosquito larvae → Tilapia → man

Which organism is properly matched with its trophic level?

Algae are the producers (first trophic level), the mosquito larvae that eat them are primary consumers, the Tilapia that eat the larvae are secondary consumers, and man is the tertiary consumer. Only B is a correct match: A is wrong because algae are producers not decomposers, C because the larvae are consumers, and D because man is a tertiary (not quaternary) consumer. **Answer: B.**
Where does the foetus develop in a pregnant woman?

The fertilised egg implants in the wall of the uterus (womb) and the foetus develops there until birth. Fertilisation takes place in the oviduct (C), but the embryo does not develop there. **Answer: A.**
Which of the following could be a consequence of depletion of the ozone layer?

The ozone layer absorbs most of the ultraviolet (UV) radiation of the sun. When it is depleted more UV reaches the earth, causing skin cancer and eye damage. CFCs (A) are the cause of the depletion, not a consequence, and the rise of greenhouse gases and temperature (B, C) concerns global warming. **Answer: D.**
A rise in the level of chlorofluorocarbons in the atmosphere.
Rise in level of greenhouse gases.
Decrease in the average temperature of the earth.
Increased exposure to dangerous UV radiation.
The small gap between adjacent Schwann cells of an axon is called:

The myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells is interrupted at regular small gaps called nodes of Ranvier, where the nerve impulse jumps from one node to the next. A synapse (A) and the synaptic cleft (D) are the junction and the gap between two neurones. **Answer: B.**
Which one of the following organs is responsible for the excretion of bile pigments?

Bile pigments (bilirubin) are formed in the liver from the breakdown of haemoglobin of worn-out red blood cells, and the liver excretes them in the bile. The gall bladder only stores and concentrates bile (A). **Answer: C.**

The diagram below shows the layout of a flush toilet. (Diagram courtesy R. H. Stone and Cozens).

![Layout of a flush toilet with water cistern, lavatory bowl, U-bend, septic tank and soak away pit (Question 31).](/media/figures/cm/gce-ol-human-biology-2018-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.webp)

What is the purpose of the water in the U-bend of this toilet?

The U-bend always holds some water. This water forms a seal (a trap) that stops foul gases and smells from the sewer and the septic tank from coming back into the house. It does not dissolve or dilute the waste (A, D). **Answer: C.**
To prevent the faeces sticking to the outlet pipe.
To stop smell from sewer entering the house.
To dilute urine and faeces not to stain the lavatory pan.
A birth control method which prevents the implantation of the fertilized egg cell is called:

An intrauterine device (IUD) placed in the uterus prevents the fertilised egg from implanting in the uterine wall. The contraceptive pill and the hormonal implant (A, D) act mainly by stopping ovulation, and tubal ligation (B) blocks the oviducts so that egg and sperm cannot meet. **Answer: C.**

Identify the food type which will likely result in kwashiorkor.
Kwashiorkor is caused by a severe lack of protein in the diet. Food D has by far the lowest protein content (0.5 g), against 23.2, 25.0 and 19 g for A, B and C. **Answer: D.**

The phenotype of an organism refers to the:

*Options as printed:* A) the physical or physiological expression of the genes of an individual.   B) genetic composition of an organism.   C) alternative forms of a gene.   D) the physical expression of the genes of an organism.

The phenotype is the observable characteristics of an organism, that is the expression of its genes (the genotype) in its environment. B describes the genotype and C describes alleles. A and D are almost identical; A is the more complete one because it also includes physiological features (for example blood group), but the two options cannot be told apart with certainty, so the question is not marked automatically.

What is the name of the hormone, which stimulates ovulation in the menstrual cycle?

A surge of luteinising hormone (LH) from the pituitary gland causes the mature follicle to release the egg (ovulation). FSH stimulates the development of the follicle (A), oestrogen repairs the uterine lining (B) and progesterone maintains it (D). **Answer: C.**
Choose the characteristic that distinguishes man from other mammals:

Man walks upright on two legs (bipedal gait), which is not true of other mammals in general. Constant body temperature, two sets of teeth in a lifetime and being warm-blooded (A, C, D) are features of mammals in general and do not separate man from them. **Answer: B.**
Maintenance of a constant body temperature.
Has two sets of teeth in life time.
A food sample tested with Sudan III solution turned red. *(The printed paper does not give the question itself; it asks which food class this shows.)*

Sudan III dissolves in fats and oils and stains them red, so a red colour shows that the sample contains fat. Reducing sugars are tested with Benedict's solution, proteins with the biuret test, and non-reducing sugars after boiling with acid. **Answer: C.**

Questions 39 and 40 consist of two statements.
Choose A if both statements are true and the second statement is a correct explanation of the first statement.
Choose B if both statements are true but the second statement is not a correct explanation of the first statement.
Choose C if the first statement is true but the second statement is false.
Choose D if both statements are false.

**Question 39**

First statement: Red blood cells have nuclei at maturity.

Second statement: Red blood cells are less numerous than white blood cells.

The first statement is false: mature red blood cells have lost their nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin. The second statement is false: red cells (about 5 million per mm³) are far more numerous than white cells (about 7 thousand per mm³). Both statements are false. **Answer: D.**
Both statements are true and the second is a correct explanation of the first
Both statements are true but the second is not a correct explanation of the first
The first statement is true but the second is false

Questions 39 and 40 consist of two statements.
Choose A if both statements are true and the second statement is a correct explanation of the first statement.
Choose B if both statements are true but the second statement is not a correct explanation of the first statement.
Choose C if the first statement is true but the second statement is false.
Choose D if both statements are false.

**Question 40**

First statement: A cross between two individuals heterozygous for albinism will result in an albino.

Second statement: Albinism is caused by a recessive allele resulting from gene mutation.

*Options as printed:* A) Both statements are true and the second is a correct explanation of the first   B) Both statements are true but the second is not a correct explanation of the first   C) The first statement is true but the second is false   D) Both statements are false

The second statement is true: albinism is caused by a recessive allele that arose by mutation, and it shows only in the homozygous recessive (aa). For the first statement, Aa × Aa gives 25 % aa (albino) and 75 % non-albino offspring, so the cross does not necessarily produce an albino; it is true only in the sense that an albino child is possible. The options do not include 'first statement false, second true', so the printed question cannot be marked automatically.

**Intended answer: the second statement is true and the first is true only in the sense that an albino child is possible (25 % of the offspring), so none of the four options fits exactly.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
A long-term effect of excessive alcohol consumption on the body is:

Years of heavy drinking damage the liver cells, which are replaced by scar tissue: this is liver cirrhosis. Slurred speech (D) is a short-term effect of drunkenness, emphysema (C) is a lung disease linked to smoking, and jaundice (B) is a sign of liver trouble, not the long-term disease. **Answer: A.**
How is lymph different from tissue fluid?

Lymph is tissue fluid that has drained into the lymph vessels. It carries more fats (absorbed from the small intestine by the lacteals) and more white blood cells (lymphocytes made in the lymph nodes) than tissue fluid. **Answer: A.**
It contains more fats and more white blood cells.
It contains more fats and less white blood cells.
It contains less fats and more white blood cells.
It contains less fats and less white blood cells.
Smooth muscles differ from cardiac muscles in that they are:

Smooth (involuntary) muscle fibres are spindle-shaped, not striated, and each has one nucleus. Cardiac muscle fibres are branched and striated. Option D is the only one that describes smooth muscle correctly (A describes cardiac muscle; B and C are wrong because smooth muscle fibres are not multinucleated). **Answer: D.**
Identify the beneficial effect of fungi to humans:

Yeast, a fungus, ferments sugar and produces carbon dioxide that makes dough rise, so it is used in bakeries to make bread. Rotting of wood and parasitism (A, D) are harmful effects, and pickling vegetables (B) is done by bacteria and acid or salt. **Answer: C.**
They are used in bakeries to make bread.
Identify the type of health unit that takes care of patients with mental problems:

A psychiatric unit treats patients with mental illness. A geriatric unit cares for old people (A) and an antenatal unit for pregnant women (D); a general hospital (C) is not specific to mental problems. **Answer: B.**
The Red Cross is a non-govermmental organisation. What is its primary role?

The Red Cross was founded to give help and first aid to the wounded and the victims of war and disasters, and this remains its primary role. Options B, C and D are not its main purpose. **Answer: A.**
To administer first-aid to war victims.
To administer first-aid to school children.
To control the spread of epidemic diseases.
To fight against female genital mutilation.
A parasitic adaptation of platyhelminthes is:

A tapeworm (a platyhelminth) holds on to the wall of the host's intestine with hooks and suckers on its scolex. It has no eyes and no mouth or teeth, and the structures used for attachment are hooks, not spines. **Answer: B.**
The presence of spines on their scolex.
The presence of hooks on their scolex.
The presence of eyes on the scolex.
The presence of teeth in their mouth.

The graph plots the level of blood glucose after a heavy meal against time. Study the graph and answer questions 48 and 49, which are based on it.

![Level of blood sugar (mg/ml of blood) against time in minutes after a heavy meal (Question 48).](/media/figures/cm/gce-ol-human-biology-2018-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.webp)

How long did it take for the blood glucose level to fall to 100 mg/ml?
On the graph the curve stays at 250 for the first part, then falls and reaches 100 mg/ml at the 90 minute mark, after which it stays level. 90 minutes is 1 hour 30 minutes. **Answer: C.**
Identify the hormone that plays a key role in the regulation of blood sugar after a heavy carbohydrate meal:

After a meal rich in carbohydrate the blood glucose rises and the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin makes the liver and muscles change glucose into glycogen and the cells use more glucose, so the level falls (as in the graph of question 48). Glucagon and adrenaline raise blood sugar (B, A). **Answer: D.**
What is the name given to pillars on which a house built in a flood-prone area is suspended?

Houses in flood-prone areas are raised on stilts, so that the floor is above the water level. Eaves (A) are the lower edge of a roof that overhangs the wall, and props (D) are temporary supports. **Answer: B.**
Which of the following input devices is the most appropriate to mark correct answers of multiple choice questions on an answer sheet?

An optical mark reader (OMR) detects the position of pencil marks on pre-printed forms, which is exactly how MCQ answer sheets are marked. A scanner (B) only produces an image, and the magnetic readers (C, D) read magnetic ink characters such as those on cheques (MICR). **Answer: A.**
What is the main advantage of networking?

The main purpose of connecting computers is to share resources: printers, files, storage, software and an Internet connection. Cost reduction (A) is a consequence of sharing, not the main advantage in itself. **Answer: B.**
A software used to prevent intruders from gaining access into networks is called a(n) ___

A firewall filters incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks unauthorised access to a network. An antivirus (A) detects and removes malicious programs, while malware (B) and spyware (D) are themselves harmful software. **Answer: C.**
A network type suitable for a large electricity corporation which has offices in all regions of the Republic of Cameroon is a ___

Offices spread over all the regions of a country are separated by hundreds of kilometres, so they are linked by a Wide Area Network (WAN). A LAN covers one building or site, a MAN covers a city, and a WLAN is a wireless LAN. **Answer: B.**

Which of the following is most likely to be true about computer networks?

*Options as printed:* A) The further apart the computers are, the slower the communication is.   B) The more the computers, the more difficult it is to communicate.   C) Virus spread more in WANs than in LANs.   D) The more the users, the more insecure the network is likely to become.

Option B is false (networks are designed to scale) and C is not a general rule (viruses spread through any connected network). The two defensible statements are A (a longer distance adds delay and usually lower speed) and D (each extra user is an extra possible source of weak passwords, infection or misuse, so the risk grows). The statement about security (D) is the one usually given in ICT courses as the general disadvantage of large networks.

**Intended answer: D (The more the users, the more insecure the network is likely to become).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
Which of the following explains the effect on a client-server network of bus topology when a client breaks down?

In a bus topology all devices hang on one shared cable. A client that breaks down (its computer fails) does not cut the cable, so the other clients and the server keep communicating. The network would fail only if the main cable itself were broken (A). Performance does not improve (D); at best the traffic is slightly reduced. **Answer: C.**
Only the computers on the side of the server function.
The other computers will improve in performance.
Select the best option if the cable of the file server in a star network breaks.

In a star network every device has its own cable to the central hub or switch. If the cable of the file server breaks, only the server is disconnected: the other computers stay connected to the hub and the network keeps working, but nobody can retrieve files stored on the server. B is wrong because the other stations do not stop. C is wrong because a disconnected server loses all its network services, Internet included. D does not happen automatically; it needs a backup server. **Answer: A.**
The network remains functional but no file can be retrieved from the server.
The system stops functioning and no file can be retrieved from the server.
All services of the server stop but its Internet services remain functional.
Another computer plays the role of the file server and the system stays on.
Information used by a router to determine the destination of each piece of data is contained in a ___

Each packet carries a header holding the source and destination addresses (IP addresses). The router reads the destination address of every packet and then looks in its routing table to choose the next hop. The configuration table (A) is stored in the router, not carried by the data; TCP/IP (B) is a set of protocols; the network board (D) is the network interface card. **Answer: C.**
The situation in which users of an intranet work together in groups using web cameras is ___

Videoconferencing uses web cameras, microphones and a network so that people in different places see and hear each other and work together as a group. Distance working (A) is working from home or a remote place without necessarily using cameras, distributed computing (C) shares processing between computers, and blogging (D) is publishing online posts. **Answer: B.**

A command line interface is different from a graphical user interface in that

*Options as printed:* A) It is not text-based.   B) Commands are given using menus.   C) It requires a mouse.   D) Doesn't require users to have knowledge of commands.

A command line interface (CLI) is text-based: the user must know and type the commands exactly (for example dir or copy), and no mouse or menu is needed. A graphical user interface (GUI) uses windows, icons, menus and a pointing device, and does not require the user to memorise commands. Every printed option describes the GUI rather than the CLI, so the question is not reliable as printed.

**Probable printed key: D, which is only true if read as a description of the graphical interface; as worded it is false for a command line interface.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
Which of the following is NOT an example of a pointing device?
A pointing device moves a pointer or selects a position on the screen: a joystick, a mouse and a light pen all do this. The keyboard is a text-entry device, so it is the odd one out. **Answer: A.**
The name given to files that have been reduced in size is ___

Compression (for example ZIP or RAR) reduces the size of a file by removing redundancy, and the result is called a compressed file. Coded and decoded files (A, D) relate to encoding or encryption, and 'shrunken file' (C) is not a technical term. **Answer: B.**
Software designed to disturb the functioning of a computer system is called a ___

A virus is malicious software that attaches itself to programs or files and disturbs, damages or slows down the normal functioning of a computer. A cookie (A) is a small text file stored by a website, spyware (C) secretly collects information, and a driver (D) is legitimate software that lets the operating system use a device. **Answer: B.**

Which of the following is a storage device?

*Options as printed:* A) Memory card reader.   B) Flash disk.   C) DVD.   D) Floppy disk.

A memory card reader is only an interface used to read a card, so A is not a storage device. However B (flash disk), C (DVD) and D (floppy disk) are all storage media or devices, so the printed question has several valid answers.

**Intended answer: B (Flash disk).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
A multimedia resource may combine several elements such as

Multimedia combines several media: text, sound, still graphics, animation and video. Option C is the only one that lists them; speakers (A) are a hardware device, not a medium, and B and D list only two media each. **Answer: C.**
Text sound, graphics, animation and video only.
Backup of data files will usually help to prevent:

A backup is a copy of the files kept elsewhere. If the originals are deleted, corrupted or destroyed, the copy can be restored, so the backup prevents permanent loss of data. It does not prevent a virus infection (A) and it creates, rather than prevents, duplicates (C). **Answer: D.**
Which software would you use to write a textbook?

A word processor (for example Microsoft Word) is used to type, format and edit long documents such as a book. A browser (A) displays web pages, a spreadsheet (B) handles calculations, and a tutorial (C) is a teaching resource, not the tool for writing. **Answer: D.**
Which of these is true of a System Development Life Cycle?

The system development life cycle (SDLC) is the series of stages (feasibility study, analysis, design, implementation, testing, maintenance...) through which a system is developed, and it is led by the system analyst. B is false (the schedule is given by a project plan such as a Gantt chart), C is false (the usual textbook cycle has five to seven phases, not eight) and D describes project management, not the SDLC. **Answer: A.**
It is managed by a system analyst.
Gives the duration of the project
It is used to manage a project.
Which of these is NOT used as a software development model?
Prototyping, the Boehm spiral model and the waterfall model are all recognised software development models. 'Navigation' is a web or user-interface notion, not a development model. **Answer: A.**
Which of the following is a low level language?

COBOL, FORTRAN and ALGOL are high-level languages with English-like statements. Assembly language, which uses mnemonics close to the machine instructions of the processor, is a low-level language. **Answer: D.**
Exactly, how many bytes are in 2.5 kilobytes?
In computing, 1 kilobyte = 1024 bytes. So 2.5 KB = 2.5 x 1024 = 2560 bytes. Option A is 256 (a decimal slip), C and D are not multiples of 1024. **Answer: B.**

The clock speed of a CPU is measured in

*Options as printed:* A) Bits per second.   B) Hertz.   C) Cycles per second.   D) Bytes per second.

The clock speed is the number of clock pulses (cycles) the processor generates each second, and it is measured in hertz (Hz), usually MHz or GHz. Bits per second (A) measure data transmission rate and bytes per second (D) measure data transfer rate. Note that one hertz is by definition one cycle per second, so B and C express the same unit and the printed question has two valid answers.

**Intended answer: B (Hertz).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
The correct order of the stages for a system development life cycle is

The system is first checked for viability (feasibility study), then the existing system and the needs are studied (analysis), the new system is planned (design) and finally built and put into use (implementation). Only option C respects this order. **Answer: C.**
In SDLC, the collection of information by means of interviews, questionnaires observation and inspection of documents is an activity in

Fact-finding techniques (interviews, questionnaires, observation, inspection of documents) are used in the analysis stage to understand how the current system works and what users need. 'System specification' (C) and 'information requirement' (D) are products of the analysis, not the stage in which facts are collected, and 'system investigation' (B) is an alternative name sometimes used for the feasibility study. **Answer: A.**
What data type do we use for a variable called FOUND which asserts the presence of an element in an array of numbers?

FOUND only has to say yes or no (the element is present or not), that is TRUE or FALSE, so the Boolean type is used. A real or integer variable stores numbers, and 'Number' is not a data type name. **Answer: B.**
An information system that manages on-line requests of hotel clients is termed a ___

A hotel booking system must answer a client at once and update the availability of rooms immediately so that two clients are not given the same room. This is real-time (online transaction) processing. A batch system (D) collects data and processes it later, a GIS (A) deals with maps and a management information system (C) summarises data for managers. **Answer: B.**
Which of the lists below contains only input devices?

The mouse, the webcam and the magnetic ink character reader (MICR) all send data to the computer. In B the printer is an output device, in C the printer and speakers are output devices, and in D the flash disk is a storage device. **Answer: A.**
Which of the following are Magnetic storage media?
Hard disks and floppy disks store data as magnetised areas on a magnetic surface. A USB flash disk uses flash (solid-state) memory, and CDs and DVDs are optical media read by a laser. **Answer: C.**
Floppy disk and USB flash disk.
A device that captures data to be processed by the computer system is called a(n)

An input device (keyboard, scanner, microphone...) captures data and sends it to the computer for processing. Storage devices keep data, and connecting or communication devices link computers together. **Answer: D.**
Which of the following best describes the purpose of a communication system?

The purpose of any communication system is to transport (transmit) data and information from a sender to a receiver. Radio, TV and telephones (A) are only examples of such systems, managing data (C) is the role of an information system, and controlling a company's activities (D) is management. **Answer: B.**

Change is the main concern of the Pre-Socratics. Assess this assertion.

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** The Pre-Socratics were the first Greek thinkers (sixth and fifth centuries BC) to explain the world by reason (*logos*) and not by myth. They asked what the world is made of and how the many changing things come from, and return to, a first principle (*arche*). The assertion to assess is that change was their main concern. The problematic is whether their thought was driven chiefly by the problem of change, or by the search for what remains permanent beneath change.

**Thesis: change was the main concern of the Pre-Socratics.**
(i) *The Milesians.* Thales (water), Anaximander (the *apeiron*, the boundless) and Anaximenes (air) wanted to explain how one principle gives rise to the many things of experience. Anaximenes explained it by condensation and rarefaction; Anaximander by the separation of opposites out of the boundless. Their question was about becoming: how do things come to be and pass away?
(ii) *Heraclitus* is the clearest case. For him everything is in flux, fire is the symbol of constant transformation, and the same river is never entered twice with the same waters. Change is not an illusion but the very nature of reality, ruled by the *logos* and by the tension of opposites.
(iii) *The pluralists* (Empedocles, Anaxagoras, the atomists Leucippus and Democritus) were mainly trying to account for change: coming-to-be and perishing were explained as the mixing and separating of eternal roots, seeds or atoms moved by Love and Strife, by Mind (*nous*) or by void and motion.
(iv) Even the Eleatics took their position because of change: Parmenides and Zeno denied it precisely because they judged it unintelligible.

**Antithesis: change was not the only or the main concern.**
(i) *The search for permanence.* Each theory above also looks for something that does not change: the arche of the Milesians, the *logos* of Heraclitus, the eternal elements of the pluralists. Change is explained by reference to something permanent.
(ii) *The Eleatics* made permanence the only reality: Parmenides argued that what is cannot come from what is not, so being is one, ungenerated and unchanging, and change belongs to the unreliable "way of opinion". Zeno's paradoxes of motion were meant to show that change and plurality are contradictory. The Eleatic challenge shaped all later Pre-Socratic thought.
(iii) *Other concerns.* The Pythagoreans studied number, harmony and the destiny of the soul; Xenophanes criticised the anthropomorphic gods and asked about the limits of knowledge; the Sophists, though later, turned to human questions of knowledge, language and the city. So the Pre-Socratics were not limited to a single problem.

**Synthesis.** Change and permanence are two sides of one problem: the relation of the one and the many. To explain change one must assume something that endures through it, and to affirm permanence one must face the evidence of change. The Pre-Socratics differ in where they put the emphasis (Heraclitus on change, Parmenides on permanence), but all try to make the changing world intelligible.

**Conclusion.** The assertion is partly right: the problem of change is central, because it is what the arche, the elements and the Eleatic denial are meant to answer. It is not fully right if it means the only concern, for permanence, the unity of the cosmos, the soul and knowledge also occupied them. It is more exact to say that their main concern was the relation between change and permanence, which later Plato and Aristotle took up.

Is belief instrumental in Peirce's Pragmatism?

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** Charles Sanders Peirce (nineteenth century, United States) is the founder of Pragmatism. In his early essays on inquiry, he treats belief not as a mere picture of the world but as something tied to action and to the settling of doubt. To say that belief is *instrumental* is to say that it is a tool, valued for what it allows us to do. The problematic is whether, for Peirce, belief is only such a tool, or whether it also aims at truth.

**Thesis: yes, belief is instrumental for Peirce.**
(i) *Doubt and belief.* For Peirce doubt is an uneasy, irritating state, and belief is a calm, satisfied state. The aim of inquiry is to pass from doubt to belief. Belief is thus what ends the irritation of doubt and allows us to act.
(ii) *Belief as a habit of action.* A belief is a rule or habit that guides what we do in given circumstances. Different beliefs are distinguished only by the different modes of action they produce. This is the heart of his pragmatic maxim: to clarify an idea, consider its conceivable practical effects.
(iii) *Methods of fixing belief.* Peirce lists four methods: tenacity (holding to what we already believe), authority (belief imposed by the state or a group), the a priori method (belief that seems agreeable to reason) and the method of science. They are compared by how well they settle belief in a stable way. Belief is therefore treated as something to be produced and secured, like an instrument.
(iv) *Meaning is practical.* An idea with no conceivable effect on conduct or experience is empty. This gives belief a practical, instrumental function.

**Antithesis: belief is not merely instrumental.**
(i) *Peirce rejects the idea that a belief is true because it is useful or comfortable.* Tenacity and authority are effective at calming doubt, yet he rejects them because they do not answer to reality; they can be broken by experience and by the clash of opinions.
(ii) *The scientific method* is preferred because it relies on something outside our will: reality, which affects all inquirers in the same way. Truth is the opinion on which inquirers would finally agree if inquiry were pushed far enough. Belief therefore aims at truth, not simply at comfort.
(iii) *Contrast with James and Dewey.* William James came to say that the true is what works (its "cash value"), and Dewey called ideas instruments of problem-solving. Peirce distanced himself from this subjective reading, and later called his own view by another name to mark the difference.
(iv) *Fallibilism.* Peirce holds that every belief is open to revision; this shows that belief answers to evidence and not only to utility.

**Synthesis.** Belief is instrumental in function (it guides action and ends doubt) but not in justification (it is correct only when the method that fixes it is answerable to reality). Peirce joins the practical and the objective: the practical meaning of a belief is what it makes us do, and its truth is what inquiry would finally settle.

**Conclusion.** For Peirce belief is instrumental in a limited sense: it is a habit of action that settles doubt. But it is not merely instrumental, since the best way of fixing it, the method of science, is chosen because it tracks reality. Pragmatism in Peirce's sense is a theory of meaning and inquiry, not a justification of any useful opinion.

"The African is notoriously religious". Assess this view of J.S. Mbiti.

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** John S. Mbiti, a Kenyan theologian and philosopher, opens his study of traditional African thought by saying that Africans are "notoriously religious": religion permeates every area of life. The problematic is whether this description is a faithful account of African worldviews, or a generalisation that hides the diversity of Africa and the place of reason in its thought.

**Thesis: the view is largely correct.**
(i) *Religion pervades life.* In traditional African societies birth, initiation, marriage, farming, healing, politics and death all have religious meaning. Mbiti says there is no sharp line between the sacred and the secular, so that wherever the African is, his religion is with him.
(ii) *Beliefs in God, spirits and ancestors.* Many African peoples have a belief in a supreme God, in divinities and spirits, and in the ancestors, whom Mbiti calls the "living-dead", still part of the community. Ritual, sacrifice, libation and prayer link the visible and invisible worlds.
(iii) *Communal and ethical dimension.* Religion supports moral order and community: the person exists through the group ("I am because we are"), and duties to the living, the dead and the unborn are religious duties.
(iv) *Concept of time.* Mbiti's analysis of time (the *sasa* and *zamani* of East African languages) is used to show that African thought is shaped by a religious sense of the past and of the ancestors.

**Antithesis: the view is open to criticism.**
(i) *Generalisation.* Africa has hundreds of peoples with different beliefs, and some societies show little interest in a high God. To speak of "the African" risks making a single type out of many.
(ii) *Hellenisation and Christian bias.* Critics such as Okot p'Bitek argue that Mbiti, trained as a Christian theologian, describes African religions with European and Christian categories (God, soul, immortality) which distort them. Others (Wiredu, Hountondji) say the claim feeds the old colonial image of the African as pre-logical and emotional, and neglects African rationality, science, technology and critical thinking.
(iii) *The word "notoriously".* It suggests excess or even a fault, while religiousness is neither a deficiency nor unique to Africa: other peoples are also deeply religious.
(iv) *Change.* Contemporary Africa has secularism, science, Islam and Christianity, and much non-religious thought; a timeless description is not enough.

**Synthesis.** Mbiti points to a real fact, the importance of the sacred in the lived world of most traditional African communities, and gives it a philosophical description. The fair reading is that religion is central in many African cultures but not exclusive: African thought also contains reason, argument and practical knowledge, and is plural.

**Conclusion.** Mbiti's view is valuable as a description of the religious character of many African societies, and it helped to make African thought a subject of study. It must be qualified by the diversity of Africa, by the risk of reading African religion through foreign categories, and by the evidence of African rationality. Religion is a major, not the only, dimension of African life.

Has Ujama'a contributed to the growth of African Social Philosophy?

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** *Ujamaa* is a Swahili word meaning familyhood or brotherhood. It is the name of the African socialism formulated by Julius Nyerere, first President of Tanzania, and made official policy by the Arusha Declaration of 1967. African social philosophy is the reflection on how African societies should be organised so as to respect human dignity, community and development. The problematic is whether Ujamaa has really enriched this reflection, or whether it is mainly a political experiment that failed.

**Thesis: Ujamaa has contributed to African social philosophy.**
(i) *A rooted theory of society.* Nyerere argued that socialism is an attitude of mind, not an import from Europe: traditional African society was already organised on the family spirit, with land held in common, mutual aid and respect for every member. Ujamaa therefore draws on African values, and rejects both capitalism, which makes the individual a competitor, and Marxist class struggle, which Nyerere said Africa did not need.
(ii) *Basic principles.* Respect for every person, common ownership of the main means of production, and the duty of everyone to work (no "parasites"). These principles give a coherent social ethic.
(iii) *Link with self-reliance and education.* The ideas of self-reliance and of education for self-reliance made development a matter of people's own effort and learning, not dependence on foreign aid.
(iv) *Influence.* Ujamaa joined Senghor's African socialism, Nkrumah's consciencism and Kaunda's humanism in a family of African thought that sought a third way between East and West and inspired debate on communalism, equality and nation-building.

**Antithesis: its contribution is limited.**
(i) *Idealisation of tradition.* Critics say Nyerere pictured the pre-colonial village as more harmonious than it was, ignoring inequalities of age, gender and rank and the presence of conflict.
(ii) *Practical failure.* The policy of ujamaa villages, which in the 1970s became compulsory resettlement, was criticised as coercive, reduced agricultural output and increased dependence on aid; the state became very powerful.
(iii) *Theoretical weakness.* Some Marxist and liberal critics found the doctrine vague, a blend of moral ideas rather than a rigorous analysis of classes, markets and power.
(iv) *Change after Nyerere.* Tanzania moved toward market reforms in the 1980s, which shows the limits of the model.

**Synthesis.** A distinction must be made between Ujamaa as an idea and Ujamaa as a policy. As a policy it was uneven and partly failed; as a philosophy it contributed lasting questions: how to build a modern society on African values of solidarity, how to join freedom with equality, and how to make development human-centred.

**Conclusion.** Yes, Ujamaa has contributed to the growth of African social philosophy by giving an original, morally grounded alternative and by stimulating the debate on African socialism, communalism and self-reliance. Its contribution lies more in ideas and moral vision than in the success of its application.

Is death the end of human existence?

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** Death is the end of biological life, but philosophers ask whether it is also the end of the person, that is, whether something of the human being survives. The problematic is whether human existence stops entirely at death, or whether the soul, the person or the spirit continues in some form.

**Thesis: death is the end of human existence.**
(i) *Materialism.* Epicurus and the atomists held that the soul, like the body, is made of atoms which disperse at death. Epicurus added that death is nothing to us: when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not. Modern materialism and neuroscience tie consciousness to brain activity: when the brain stops, consciousness stops.
(ii) *Empiricism.* Hume noted that we have no experience of a soul apart from the body and no evidence of survival, so the belief is not supported by reason.
(iii) *Dependence of mind on body.* Memory, character and thought change with injury, drugs or illness, which suggests that the mind depends on the body.
(iv) *Existentialist reading.* For Sartre death is not a gate to another life but the end of the possibilities of the person, absurd and outside any project; for Heidegger, man is a being-toward-death, whose finitude gives life its seriousness and urgency, without a promise of survival.

**Antithesis: death is not the end.**
(i) *The immortality of the soul.* Plato (in the *Phaedo*) argued that the soul is simple, akin to the eternal Forms, and therefore outlasts the body, which is composite. Descartes held that the mind is a distinct, thinking substance, separable from the body. Kant presented the immortality of the soul as a postulate of practical reason, needed so that virtue may be proportioned to happiness.
(ii) *Religious doctrines.* Christianity and Islam teach resurrection and judgment; Hinduism and Buddhism teach rebirth. These doctrines rest on faith and revelation.
(iii) *African thought.* Many African traditions hold that death is a passage: the dead become ancestors, called by Mbiti the living-dead, who remain members of the community as long as they are remembered, and may be reborn in the family. Life is a continuous circle that includes the ancestors.
(iv) *Objections to materialism.* Critics say it does not explain consciousness, personal identity and freedom, and that the argument from dependence on the brain only shows that the mind is conditioned by the body, not that it is identical to it.

**Synthesis.** The question mixes what can be shown by experience (death ends bodily life and the functions of the brain) with what depends on metaphysical or religious belief (whether something survives). Neither position can be demonstrated conclusively. What the options share is that the thought of death makes us consider the value of life and of how it is lived.

**Conclusion.** Philosophy cannot prove with certainty that death is, or is not, the end of human existence. The materialist and existentialist answer is the best supported by observation; the dualist, religious and African answers are supported by arguments about the soul and by faith. A reasonable position acknowledges the limits of proof and treats the question as one on which the arguments are balanced.

Can man be held responsible for his acts?

(25 marks)

**Introduction.** To hold someone responsible is to judge that he is the author of his act and so deserves praise or blame, reward or punishment. This presupposes that he could have acted otherwise, that is, that he is free. The problematic is whether man, who is subject to nature, heredity, upbringing and society, can really be held responsible for his acts.

**Thesis: man can be held responsible.**
(i) *Freedom of the will.* Libertarians, such as Sartre, hold that man is free: existence precedes essence, man makes himself by his choices and cannot hide behind excuses, for even refusing to choose is a choice. Kant holds that, as a rational being, man is able to follow the moral law, and the very sense of duty (you ought, therefore you can) shows that he is free.
(ii) *Voluntary acts.* Aristotle distinguishes voluntary acts, which have their origin in the agent who knows what he does, from involuntary ones, done through force or ignorance. For voluntary acts, including those of character built by habit, man is responsible.
(iii) *Social necessity.* Without responsibility there would be no morality, law, justice or punishment, and no praise for good conduct. Society treats persons as accountable; it is a condition of living together.
(iv) *Conscience.* We feel guilt, remorse and pride about our acts, which shows that we regard ourselves as their authors.

**Antithesis: man cannot (fully) be held responsible.**
(i) *Determinism.* Spinoza and, in different forms, modern science hold that every event has causes. If our choices are caused by heredity, environment, unconscious drives (Freud) and social conditions (Marx), then the feeling of freedom is an illusion, as Spinoza said of a stone that thinks it flies freely.
(ii) *Limits of responsibility.* Even the law recognises that children, the insane, and persons acting under constraint, threat or ignorance are not or are less responsible. Passion, addiction, poverty and manipulation reduce freedom.
(iii) *Fate.* Some religious doctrines of predestination, and some Greek and African ideas of destiny, suggest that the outcome of our acts is not wholly in our control.
(iv) *Punishment.* If acts are determined, blame is unjust and punishment should aim at reform or protection, not retribution.

**Synthesis.** Compatibilists such as Hume and Mill reconcile the two: freedom is not absence of causes but acting from one's own motives without external compulsion, so a person can be responsible for acts that flow from his character and choices, even if these have causes. Responsibility is then a matter of degree: it is full when the act is voluntary, informed and uncoerced, and reduced by constraint, ignorance or illness.

**Conclusion.** Man can be held responsible for his acts, but within limits. Total responsibility ignores the weight of conditioning, and total determinism removes the basis of morality and law. The most defensible view is that man is responsible to the extent that he acts knowingly and freely, and that society should judge each case by this measure.

Describe an experiment to determine the refractive index of a glass block. Include in your description:

- a list of apparatus needed
- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure you will use
- the precautions to be taken *[6 marks]*

**Apparatus:** a rectangular glass block, a soft-board (drawing board), a white sheet of paper, drawing pins, four optical (search) pins, a sharp pencil, a protractor, a ruler, a set square.

**Diagram of the set-up** (described): the paper is pinned on the soft-board and the glass block lies on it. Its outline $ABCD$ is drawn. A normal $NN'$ is drawn at point $O$ on face $AB$. A line $PO$ making an angle $i$ with the normal represents the incident ray. Pins $P_1$ and $P_2$ are stuck upright on the line $PO$, about $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart. Looking through face $CD$, pins $P_3$ and $P_4$ are placed so that the four pins appear exactly in line. The line through $P_3$ and $P_4$ meets $CD$ at $O'$. Join $O$ to $O'$: this is the ray inside the glass.

**Procedure:** (1) Fix the paper, place the block and trace its outline. (2) Draw the normal at $O$ and the incident line making an angle $i$ (for example $30^\circ$) with it. (3) Fix $P_1$ and $P_2$ on the incident line. (4) Looking through the opposite face, fix $P_3$ and $P_4$ so that they hide the images of $P_1$ and $P_2$ (all four in line). (5) Remove the block and the pins, draw the emergent line through $P_3$, $P_4$ and join $O$ to $O'$. (6) Draw the normal at $O$ on the inside of the glass and measure the angle of refraction $r$ (the angle between $OO'$ and the normal). (7) Calculate $n=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$. **Precautions:** the pins must be fixed **vertically** and **far apart** (at least $5\,\mathrm{cm}$) to give an accurate line; use a **sharp pencil** and a thin outline; keep the block **still** while tracing and sighting; look at the **bases of the pins** when aligning them; do not use too small or too large angles of incidence; keep the eye at table level; use a **protractor with care**, reading to the nearest degree.

A converging lens has a focal length of $50\,\mathrm{cm}$. An object is placed $80\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the lens and an image is produced on a wall $240\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the lens.

(i) Calculate the magnification of this image. *[2 marks]*

(ii) State the nature and orientation of this image. *[2 marks]*

(iii) What property of light is responsible for the formation of this image by the lens? *[2 marks]*

(i) $\text{magnification}=\dfrac{\text{image distance}}{\text{object distance}}=\dfrac{v}{u}=\dfrac{240\,\mathrm{cm}}{80\,\mathrm{cm}}=3$

**The magnification is $3$** (the image is three times as tall as the object; it has no unit).

(ii) The image falls on a wall, so it can be received on a screen: it is a **real** image. A real image formed by a converging lens is **inverted** (upside down). It is also **magnified** (enlarged).

(iii) The property is the **refraction** of light: the rays change direction (bend) when they pass from air into the glass and from the glass back into air, and the lens shape makes them converge to form the image.

(i) Define the specific latent heat of a substance. State its unit. *[3 marks]*

(ii) Name a substance with a high specific latent heat. State one use of this substance which is due to its high specific latent heat. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Explain why a burn from steam at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is more severe than one from boiling water at the same temperature. *[2 marks]*

(i) The **specific latent heat** of a substance is the **quantity of heat energy required to change unit mass (1 kg) of the substance from one state to another (solid to liquid, or liquid to gas) without any change of temperature**. Its unit is the **joule per kilogram, $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$**.

(ii) **Water** (specific latent heat of vaporisation about $2.3\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$). Use: steam is used to **heat or sterilise** (steam pipes, autoclaves, cooking), because each kilogram of steam gives out a very large amount of heat when it condenses. (Other accepted answer: ice is used to **cool drinks and preserve food** because it absorbs a large amount of heat when it melts.)

(iii) Steam at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ **gives out its latent heat of vaporisation as it condenses on the skin**, in addition to the heat given out as the water formed cools. Boiling water at the same temperature gives out only the second amount. Steam therefore delivers **much more heat energy per kilogram** to the skin and causes a more severe burn.

(i) Describe an experiment to show that different materials (solids) conduct heat at different rates.

- A list of apparatus needed
- A diagram of the set-up
- The procedure you will use
- The precautions to be taken *[5 marks]*

(ii) Name three situations in which these differences in conductivity between different materials are put to use. *[3 marks]*

(i) **Apparatus:** rods of the **same length and diameter** made of different metals (for example copper, aluminium, iron and brass), candle wax (or petroleum jelly), small ball bearings or drawing pins, a Bunsen burner, a tripod and a stand, a stop-watch, matches.

**Diagram of the set-up** (described): the rods are fixed in a **star arrangement** (or side by side), their inner ends together over the Bunsen flame and their free ends outwards on supports. A drawing pin is stuck with a little wax at the same distance from the heated end of each rod.

**Procedure:** attach one drawing pin to each rod with the same quantity of wax, at equal distances from the flame. Heat the joined ends **at the same time** with the burner. Heat travels along each rod; the wax melts and the pin falls when the heat reaches it. Note the order in which the pins fall (or the time each pin takes to fall). The pin on the **copper** rod falls first, then aluminium, brass, and the iron rod last, which shows that the metals conduct heat at different rates (copper is the best conductor).

**Precautions:** use rods of the **same length and thickness**; use the **same size of pin and amount of wax**; heat all the rods **at the same time and equally**, the flame being shielded from draughts; handle the hot apparatus with care and keep the rods well supported.

(ii) Any three of: **cooking pots and pans made of metal** (aluminium or copper) with **wooden or plastic handles**; **soldering iron** with a copper tip and an insulating handle; **electric wires covered with plastic or rubber** (heat and electrical insulation); **lagging of hot water pipes and tanks** with poor conductors; **oven gloves** made of cloth; **clothes** (woollen clothes keep the body warm because trapped air is a poor conductor); **houses with roofs or ceilings** made of poor conductors.

A student noticed that when fire is burning in a firewood kitchen, cold air flows into the kitchen through the door while the smoke moves out through a hole high up in the wall.

(i) Name the phenomenon that causes this observation. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Briefly explain how this observation occurs. *[3 marks]*

(iii) Name one daily occurrence due to this phenomenon. *[1 mark]*

(i) **Convection** (a convection current).

(ii) The fire heats the air in the kitchen. This air **expands, becomes less dense** and **rises**, carrying the smoke with it, and leaves the kitchen through the hole high up in the wall. **Cooler, denser air** from outside flows in through the door at the bottom to take the place of the air that has left. A circulating current of air is set up.

(iii) Any one of: a **sea breeze** or **land breeze**; the **ventilation** of rooms and the working of a **chimney**; the heating of water in a **kettle or pot**; the working of a **refrigerator** (cold air sinking) or a hot-water **cylinder**.

(i) What is an elastic material? *[1 mark]*

(ii) State Hooke's law. *[2 marks]*

(i) An **elastic material** is one that **returns to its original shape and size when the force that deformed it is removed** (for example a steel spring or a rubber band within its limit).

(ii) **Hooke's law:** the **extension of an elastic material is directly proportional to the stretching force applied to it, provided the elastic limit (limit of proportionality) is not exceeded**; that is, $F\propto e$ or $F=ke$.

State the energy changes that occur from the moment a stone is released at a height to the moment it comes to rest on the ground. *[3 marks]*

1. While the stone falls, its **gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy** (the stone speeds up; in air a small part is changed into heat by air resistance).
2. At the instant it hits the ground the **kinetic energy is at its maximum** (equal to the potential energy lost, if air resistance is ignored).
3. As the stone stops on the ground, its **kinetic energy changes into heat energy and sound energy** (and a little work to deform the ground/stone). The total energy is conserved.

$^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Ra}$ is one of the **isotopes** of randon with a **half-life** of $3.8$ days. It undergoes radioactivity by alpha particle emission resulting in a **transmutation** process. Define each of the underlined terms or expressions. *[3 marks]*

- **Isotopes:** atoms of the **same element** (same proton number $Z$) that have **different numbers of neutrons**, so different mass numbers.
- **Half-life:** the **time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay** (equivalently, for the activity or count rate to fall to half).
- **Transmutation:** the **change of one element into another** when a nucleus emits a particle. In alpha decay the proton number falls by $2$ and the mass number by $4$: $^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn}\rightarrow{}^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po}+{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$.

Alpha particle tracks in a cloud chamber are **thick**, **straight** and **short**, while beta-particles tracks are **thin**, **wavy** and **long**. State the reason for each of the characteristics underlined above. *[6 marks]*

**Alpha tracks**

- **Thick:** an alpha particle has a **large charge ($+2$) and a large mass**, so it is **strongly ionising**: it produces many ions per millimetre of path, and the droplets that form on them make a thick track.
- **Straight:** an alpha particle is **heavy**, so collisions with air molecules hardly deflect it.
- **Short:** because it ionises so strongly it **loses its energy quickly**, so it travels only a few centimetres in air.

**Beta tracks**

- **Thin:** a beta particle has a **small charge ($-1$) and a very small mass** and moves very fast, so it is **weakly ionising** and produces few ions per millimetre.
- **Wavy:** it is **very light**, so collisions with air molecules **deflect it easily** and it changes direction.
- **Long:** because it ionises weakly it **loses energy slowly** and travels much farther (metres in air) before it stops.

Figure 4.0 shows a negatively charged polythene rod brought close to an uncharged suspended metal coated ball. It is observed that the ball moves.

![Metal coated ball hanging by a thread from a support, with a horizontal charged polythene rod (dashed line inside) to the right of the ball; labels 'Metal coated ball' (arrow) and 'Charged Polythene rod'.](/media/figures/cm/gce-ol-physics-2018-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_1.webp)

*Figure 4*

(i) In which direction does the ball move? *[1 mark]*

(ii) What type of force exists between them? *[1 mark]*

(iii) Name two factors that affect the magnitude of this force. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Explain how the movement in (i) comes about. *[2 marks]*

(v) Why is it easier to charge a polythene rod than to charge a copper rod? *[2 marks]*

(i) The ball moves **towards the rod** (to the right in Figure 4): it is attracted.

(ii) A force of **electrostatic attraction**.

(iii) The **size of the charges** (the larger the charge on the rod or the ball, the larger the force) and the **distance between them** (the force decreases when the distance increases). The medium between them also matters.

(iv) The negative rod **repels the free electrons** of the metal coating of the ball, which move to the **side of the ball farthest from the rod**. The **near side is left with a positive charge** (induced charge) and the far side is negative. The attraction between the rod and the nearer, positive side is **stronger than the repulsion** from the farther, negative side (the force is larger at a smaller distance). The net force on the ball is therefore an attraction, and the ball moves towards the rod.

(v) **Polythene is an insulator**: the charge produced by rubbing stays where it is made and cannot flow away. **Copper is a conductor**: the charge produced by rubbing flows through the rod and the hand to the earth, so a copper rod held in the hand cannot be charged (unless it is held with an insulating handle).

(i) A current of $10\,\mathrm{A}$ means that a **charge of $10$ coulombs passes any point of the conductor every second** ($10\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$).

(ii) Charge that flows: $Q=It=10\,\mathrm{A}\times8\,\mathrm{s}=80\,\mathrm{C}$.

List two ways by which electrical energy could be lost in a transformer and in each case explain how this loss could be minimised. *[4 marks]*

1. **Heating of the coils (resistance of the windings, $I^2R$ loss):** the current heats the copper wire. It is minimised by **using thick copper wire of low resistance** for the coils (especially the low-voltage, high-current coil).

2. **Eddy currents in the iron core:** the changing magnetic flux induces currents in the core, which heat it. They are minimised by **making the core of thin, insulated sheets (laminations)** instead of a solid block.

(Other accepted losses: **hysteresis** loss, minimised by using a **soft iron core** that is easily magnetised and demagnetised; **flux leakage**, minimised by winding the secondary coil **on top of the primary** on a closed core.)

(i) When the conductor AB is moved upwards between the poles, it **cuts the magnetic field lines** (the magnetic flux linked with the circuit changes). By **electromagnetic induction** an **e.m.f. is induced** in AB. Because AB is part of a **closed circuit** with the galvanometer, an **induced current flows** and the pointer deflects.

(ii) The pointer **deflects in the opposite direction** (to the other side of the zero). When the direction of motion of the conductor is reversed, the **direction of the induced e.m.f. and current is reversed** (Fleming's right-hand rule / Lenz's law: the induced current always opposes the motion, so changing the motion changes its direction).

(iii) Any two of: the **speed** at which the conductor is moved; the **strength of the magnetic field (strength of the magnets)**; the **length of the conductor** in the field (or the number of turns if it is a coil).

(iv) The **right-hand grip rule** (Maxwell's corkscrew rule): grip the conductor with the right hand, thumb pointing along the current; the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines.

Distinguish between a hard magnetic material and a soft magnetic material giving an example of each. *[4 marks]*

Figure 7.0 shows three rectangular metal blocks A, B, and C. Block A is a permanent magnet of known polarity, B is a magnetic material and C another permanent magnet.

*Figure 7*

Explain how you would use block A to show a group of form 5 students that B is a magnetic material and C a permanent magnet. *[3 marks]*

**Hard and soft magnetic materials**

- A **hard magnetic material** is **difficult to magnetise but keeps its magnetism for a long time** (it is hard to demagnetise). Example: **steel** (also alnico, cobalt steel). It is used for permanent magnets.
- A **soft magnetic material** is **easily magnetised and easily demagnetised**: it loses its magnetism as soon as the magnetising field is removed. Example: **soft iron**. It is used for the cores of electromagnets and transformers.

**Using block A (a bar magnet, N at the left end and S at the right end)**

- **To show that C is a permanent magnet:** bring the **north pole of A near one end of C, then near the other end**. A permanent magnet will **repel** at one of its ends (like poles repel) and attract at the other. Repulsion is the only sure test for a magnet.
- **To show that B is a magnetic material (not a magnet):** bring the same pole of A near **each end of B in turn**. B is **attracted at both ends** and is **never repelled**; B is a magnetic material that becomes an induced magnet (nearest end gets an opposite pole) and loses its magnetism when A is removed.

Any non-zero number raised to the power $0$ equals $1$, whatever its sign: $(-5)^0=1$. The traps are to read the exponent $0$ as 'the result is $0$' (option C) or to keep the base or its sign (options A and B). **Answer: D.**

Add the like terms: $\log 2+2\log 2=3\log 2$. By the power law, $3\log 2=\log 2^3=\log 8$. Check: $\log 2\approx0.3010$, so $3\log 2\approx0.9031=\log 8$. The trap is to multiply inside the logarithm without the power law, which gives $\log 6$ (option B) or $\log 3$ (option C) by adding the numbers 2 and 1. **Answer: A.**
$(3+\sqrt2)^2$ in the form $a+b\sqrt2$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants is:

Expand: $(3+\sqrt2)^2=3^2+2\cdot3\cdot\sqrt2+(\sqrt2)^2=9+6\sqrt2+2=11+6\sqrt2$. So $a=11$ and $b=6$. The trap is to forget the middle term and write $9+2=11$ (option A), or to add $4$ instead of $2$ for $(\sqrt2)^2$ (option C: $13$). **Answer: B.**
The sum and product of the roots respectively of the quadratic equation $2x^2-x-2=0$ are:

For $ax^2+bx+c=0$ the sum of the roots is $-\dfrac ba$ and the product is $\dfrac ca$. Here $a=2$, $b=-1$, $c=-2$, so the sum is $-\dfrac{-1}{2}=\dfrac12$ and the product is $\dfrac{-2}{2}=-1$. The traps are the sign of the sum (option A has $-\frac12$) and the sign of the product (option D has $+1$). **Answer: B.**
The quadratic equation whose roots are $-2$ and $3$ is:

Use $(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=0$ with $\alpha=-2$ and $\beta=3$: $(x+2)(x-3)=x^2-3x+2x-6=x^2-x-6=0$. Check with the sum and product: sum $=-2+3=1$ gives the coefficient $-1$ of $x$, product $=-6$ gives the constant term. The trap is a sign error on the sum (option B gives $x^2+x-6$, whose roots are $2$ and $-3$). **Answer: A.**
Given that $ax^2+bx+c=0$ has real and distinct roots where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are real constants, then which of the following is correct?

The nature of the roots is decided by the discriminant $\Delta=b^2-4ac$: $\Delta>0$ gives two real and distinct roots, $\Delta=0$ gives two equal real roots and $\Delta<0$ gives no real roots. 'Real and distinct' therefore means $b^2-4ac>0$. Option A ($\geq0$) also allows equal roots, so it is not specific enough. **Answer: B.**
Which of the following is a factor of $x^3+x^2-4x-4$?

Given that $2x^2-3x+p\equiv(2x-1)(x+2)+7$, the value of $p$ is:

*Options as printed:* A) $-5$   B) $-3$   C) $3$   D) $5$

Expand the right-hand side: $(2x-1)(x+2)+7=2x^2+4x-x-2+7=2x^2+3x+5$. For the identity to hold, the coefficients of $x$ must match: $-3$ on the left against $+3$ on the right, which is impossible as printed. The question is only consistent if the left-hand side is $2x^2+3x+p$ (misprint of the sign of $3x$): then $p=5$.

The $n^{th}$ term of a series is given by $T_n=(-1)^n2^{n-1}$. Then the $5^{th}$ term is:
Substitute $n=5$: $T_5=(-1)^5\cdot2^{5-1}=(-1)\cdot2^4=-16$. The traps are to forget the sign $(-1)^5=-1$ (option C, $16$) or to use $2^5$ instead of $2^{n-1}$ (option A, $-32$). **Answer: B.**
The sum, $S_n$, of an arithmetic progression is $n(2-n)$. The $4^{th}$ term is:

The $n^{th}$ term is $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$. So $T_4=S_4-S_3=4(2-4)-3(2-3)=4(-2)-3(-1)=-8+3=-5$. Check: $S_1=1$, $S_2=0$, $S_3=-3$, $S_4=-8$, so the terms are $1,-1,-3,-5$ with common difference $-2$. The trap is to take $S_4=-8$ as the term (option B). **Answer: C.**
The fifth term of the geometric series $1+\dfrac23+\dfrac49+\cdots$ is:

The first term is $a=1$ and the common ratio is $r=\dfrac{2/3}{1}=\dfrac23$ (check: $\dfrac{4/9}{2/3}=\dfrac23$). The $n^{th}$ term is $ar^{n-1}$, so $T_5=\left(\dfrac23\right)^4=\dfrac{16}{81}$. The trap is to use the power $5$ instead of $4$, which gives $\dfrac{32}{243}$ (option B). **Answer: C.**
The sum to infinity of the series $3+1+\dfrac13+\cdots$ is:

This is a geometric series with $a=3$ and $r=\dfrac13$. Since $|r|<1$ the sum to infinity exists: $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=\dfrac{3}{1-\frac13}=\dfrac{3}{\frac23}=\dfrac92$. The trap is to compute $\dfrac{a}{r}$ or $\dfrac{a}{1+r}$ (option C is $\dfrac{13}{3}=3+1+\dfrac13$, the sum of the first three terms). **Answer: A.**
The first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, in the binomial expansion of $(1+x)^{-2}$ are:

For a negative index, $(1+x)^n=1+nx+\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2+\cdots$ with $n=-2$: the second term is $-2x$ and the third is $\dfrac{(-2)(-3)}{2}x^2=3x^2$. So $(1+x)^{-2}=1-2x+3x^2-\cdots$ (valid for $|x|<1$). Check with $x=0.1$: $1.1^{-2}=0.8264$ and $1-0.2+0.03=0.83$. The signs alternate because the index is negative. **Answer: B.**
The coefficient of $x^2$ in the binomial expansion of $(1-3x)^{-1}$ is:

Put $n=-1$ and replace $x$ by $-3x$: $(1+u)^{-1}=1-u+u^2-\cdots$ with $u=-3x$ gives $1+3x+9x^2+27x^3+\cdots$. So the coefficient of $x^2$ is $(-3)^2=9$. The trap is to forget that $(-3x)^2=+9x^2$ (options A and B) or to multiply by the binomial coefficient $2$ (option D, $18$). **Answer: C.**
${}^nP_r=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$, so ${}^4P_2=\dfrac{4!}{2!}=\dfrac{24}{2}=12$ (also $4\times3=12$). The trap is to divide by $r!$ as well, which gives ${}^4C_2=6$ (option B). **Answer: C.**
The number of ways in which three books can be selected from five books is:

$\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ are both positive in the:

By the ASTC rule, in the first quadrant ($0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$) all ratios are positive; in the second only $\sin$ is positive, in the third only $\tan$ and in the fourth only $\cos$. So both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ are positive only in the first quadrant. **Answer: A.**

Apply the double angle formula to $\tan(x+x)=\dfrac{\tan x+\tan x}{1-\tan x\tan x}=\dfrac{2\tan x}{1-\tan^2x}$. The value of $x$, $0\leq x\leq180^\circ$ for which $\cos2x=\dfrac12$ is:

A linear transformation $T:(x,y)\to(2x+y,\,3x)$. The matrix of the transformation $T$ is:

The matrix has as its rows the coefficients of $x$ and $y$ in each component of the image: $2x+y=(2)x+(1)y$ gives the first row $(2\ \ 1)$ and $3x=(3)x+(0)y$ gives the second row $(3\ \ 0)$. The invariant line under the transformation $M$, where $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&4\end{pmatrix}$ is:

Which of the following is the main function of collenchyma and sclerenchyma in plants?

Collenchyma (living, with cellulose thickening at the corners) supports young stems and petioles, and sclerenchyma (dead, with lignified walls) gives rigidity and strength to mature organs. Neither stores food, and the transport of water and of food is done by xylem and phloem. Their main function is support. **Answer: B.**
The inhibition of lateral buds by the presence of shoot tips is called:

The shoot apex produces auxin (IAA), which moves down the stem and inhibits the growth of the axillary (lateral) buds, so the plant grows tall and unbranched. This is apical dominance. When the tip is removed the lateral buds grow. Grafting, cuttings and marcotting (air layering) are methods of artificial vegetative propagation. **Answer: C.**
Impulses to the Purkinje tissue take rise from the:

The sino-atrial node (SAN) starts each heartbeat and the wave of excitation spreads over the atria to the atrio-ventricular node (AVN). After a short delay the AVN passes the impulse down the bundle of His and its branches to the Purkinje fibres in the ventricular walls, which make the ventricles contract from the apex upwards. The impulse to the Purkinje tissue therefore comes from the AVN (via the bundle of His). The SAN acts only at the start of the chain, and the brain and the vagus nerve only modify the rate. **Answer: A.**
Which of the following takes place during inspiration?

During inspiration the external intercostal muscles contract while the internal intercostals relax, so the ribs move upwards and outwards, and the diaphragm contracts and flattens. The volume of the thorax increases, the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. Options B, C and D describe the relaxation of the external intercostals or the contraction of the internal ones, which belongs to expiration. **Answer: A.**
The external intercostal muscles contract and ribs are moved upwards and outwards.
The internal intercostal muscles relax and ribs move inwards and downwards.
The external intercostal muscles relax and ribs move downwards and inwards.
The internal intercostal muscles contract and ribs move upwards and outwards.
Which of the following is associated with nitrogen fixation in bacterial cells?

The genes for nitrogen fixation (the nif genes) of nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium are carried on plasmids (the symbiotic plasmid), and plasmids are the vectors used to transfer these genes between bacteria. The photosynthetic membranes belong to photosynthetic bacteria, and the pili are used for attachment and conjugation. The bacterial chromosome also carries essential genes, but the plasmid is the structure classically associated with nitrogen fixation in this syllabus. **Answer: C.**
Above which temperature do human enzymes begin to denature?

Human enzymes work best near body temperature (37 °C). Above about 40 °C the weak hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the tertiary structure begin to break, the active site loses its shape and the activity falls; by 50 to 60 °C most enzymes are completely and irreversibly denatured. 37 °C is the optimum, not a denaturing temperature, so the temperature above which denaturation begins is 40 °C. **Answer: B.**
The force that holds liquids in a continuous stream is called:

Cohesion is the attraction between molecules of the same substance. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules hold them together in an unbroken column (as in the xylem vessels), so the stream does not break. Adhesion is attraction between water and the walls of the vessel, transpiration pull is the suction created by evaporation from the leaves, and root pressure is a push from the roots. **Answer: A.**

Humans have three different types of pigments for carriage of oxygen. These pigments vary in their capacities to carry oxygen as depicted by the curves below.

The three pigments differ in their affinity for oxygen. A curve shifted to the left reaches a given saturation at a lower partial pressure of oxygen, so it belongs to the pigment with the highest affinity. Myoglobin (in muscle) has the highest affinity of the three, foetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity than adult haemoglobin so that it can take oxygen from the mother's blood in the placenta, and normal (adult) haemoglobin has the lowest affinity, so its curve is farthest to the right. At the marked partial pressure (about 30 mm Hg) the curve X is about 70 % saturated, Y about 50 % and Z about 37 %. Therefore X = myoglobin, Y = foetal haemoglobin, Z = normal haemoglobin. **Answer: A.**
X = myoglobin; Y = foetal haemoglobin; Z = normal haemoglobin.
